notes.B: Stylopharyngeus descends between the carotid arteries towards the lateral pharyngeal wall.
notes.C: Styloglossus passes forwards from the styloid process between the carotid arteries towards the tongue.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve descends between the carotid arteries on its way towards the pharynx and tongue.
notes.E: The vagus trunk remains within the carotid sheath; its pharyngeal branch may pass between the arteries.

ana-g16-c25.why: The inferior thyroid artery usually arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the first part of the subclavian artery. The superior thyroid artery, in contrast, usually arises from the external carotid.

notes.B: The superior thyroid artery typically arises near the beginning of the external carotid and supplies the thyroid's upper pole.
notes.C: The facial artery arises from the external carotid and supplies superficial structures of the face and submandibular region.
notes.D: The lingual artery is an anterior branch of the external carotid that supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth.
notes.E: The occipital artery arises posteriorly from the external carotid and supplies the posterior scalp and adjacent muscles.

ana-g16-c43.why: The facial artery winds around the inferior border of the mandible immediately anterior to masseter. Its superficial position against bone permits palpation or compression at this point.

notes.A: The superficial temporal artery can be palpated anterior to the ear as it crosses the zygomatic arch.
notes.B: The lingual artery runs deep towards the tongue, including a segment deep to hyoglossus, rather than crossing the mandible.
notes.C: The maxillary artery runs deep within the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae rather than across the mandibular border.
notes.D: The transverse facial artery runs across the cheek below the zygomatic arch, not around the lower mandibular border.

ana-g16-p39.why: The testicular artery descends retroperitoneally towards the deep inguinal ring and travels through the inguinal canal to the scrotum. Unlike the ovarian artery, it does not normally enter the true pelvic cavity.

notes.A: The internal iliac artery descends into the true pelvis and provides the principal arterial supply to pelvic structures.
notes.B: The median sacral artery descends in the midline over the anterior sacrum, entering the pelvic cavity.
notes.C: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and descends into the pelvis to supply the rectum.
notes.D: The ovarian artery passes across the pelvic brim and runs in the suspensory ligament of the ovary to its pelvic destination.

ana-g16-p60.why: The superior gluteal artery is usually a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. It exits through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve.

notes.B: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the obturator internus tendon and returning pudendal neurovascular structures, not the superior gluteal artery.
notes.C: The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve and vessels from the pelvis into the medial thigh.
notes.D: The pudendal canal carries internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve along the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.
notes.E: The sacral foramina carry sacral nerve branches and associated vessels rather than the superior gluteal arterial trunk.

ana-g16-k84.why: The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox over the scaphoid and trapezium. Much of the scaphoid receives blood entering distally, making the proximal fragment vulnerable after a waist fracture.

notes.A: The ulnar artery passes into the hand on the ulnar side of the wrist rather than crossing the snuffbox.
notes.B: The radial artery provides branches to the scaphoid, many of which enter its distal region and supply it retrogradely.
notes.C: Thenar branches supply the thumb-side palmar muscles; the main vessel crossing the snuffbox is the radial artery.

ana-g16-t23.why: The thoracic wall is supplied chiefly by anterior and posterior intercostal arteries. The internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries supply anterior intercostal spaces, while the thoracic aorta supplies most posterior spaces.

notes.A: The internal thoracic artery gives anterior intercostal branches to the upper intercostal spaces.
notes.B: The inferior epigastric artery principally supplies the anterior abdominal wall, although it anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery.
notes.C: Posterior intercostal arteries supply the intercostal spaces, with most arising directly from the thoracic aorta.
notes.D: The thyrocervical trunk sends branches to the neck and scapula. The upper posterior intercostal supply comes via the costocervical trunk.
notes.E: The suprascapular artery chiefly supplies the scapular region rather than the intercostal muscles.

ana-ms15-27.why: Large elastic arteries accommodate pulsatile ventricular ejection through elastic lamellae, whereas muscular arteries regulate distribution through smooth muscle. All ordinary arterial lumina are lined by endothelium rather than mesothelium.

notes.A: Elastic lamellae in conducting arteries permit expansion during systole and recoil during diastole.
notes.B: Successive arterial branches generally become smaller in diameter as they approach the capillary beds.
notes.C: Smooth muscle predominates in muscular arteries, whereas elastic arteries contain abundant elastic lamellae.
notes.D: Endothelium lines blood vessels; mesothelium lines serous cavities such as the pleural cavity.
notes.E: Ordinary arteries lack serial valves because pressure gradients drive their flow; semilunar heart valves are at the ventricular outlets.

ana-ms15-28.why: The fibrous pericardium surrounds the heart in the middle mediastinum and anchors it to the central tendon and sternum. The parietal serous pericardium adheres to its inner surface.

notes.A: The anterior mediastinum lies between the sternum and anterior surface of the fibrous pericardium.
notes.B: The fibrous pericardium blends with the central tendon around the caval opening, anchoring the heart to the diaphragm.
notes.C: Sternopericardial ligaments attach the fibrous pericardium to the posterior surface of the sternum.
notes.D: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and in front of the thoracic vertebral column.
notes.E: The parietal serous pericardium is firmly adherent to the fibrous pericardium, rather than loosely attached.

ana-ms15-29.why: Serous pericardial reflections around arterial and venous roots create the transverse and oblique sinuses. The visceral and parietal layers are continuous at these reflections, enclosing a potential fluid-filled cavity.

notes.A: The serous layers reflect into each other around arterial roots; the tunica intima lines the vessel lumen separately.
notes.B: The transverse sinus lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the superior vena cava.
notes.C: The oblique sinus forms between serous reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava, rather than from the sinus venosus.
notes.D: The parietal and visceral serous layers remain continuous where they reflect around the venous roots.
notes.E: The oblique sinus is a blind recess posterior to the left atrium between the pulmonary venous reflections.

ana-ms15-30.why: Cardiac surfaces are named according to their anatomical relationships: sternocostal, diaphragmatic and pulmonary surfaces, with the posterior base largely formed by the left atrium. No standard medial surface is described.

notes.A: The posterior base is formed mainly by the left atrium and receives the pulmonary veins.
notes.B: The sternocostal surface faces the anterior thoracic wall and is formed largely by the right ventricle.
notes.C: The diaphragmatic surface rests on the diaphragm and consists chiefly of the left ventricle with part of the right ventricle.
notes.D: The left pulmonary surface faces the left lung and is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
notes.E: A distinct medial surface is not part of the standard anatomical description of the heart.

ana-ms15-31.why: The sternocostal surface faces the sternum and costal cartilages and is formed mainly by the right ventricle. It displays anterior coronary grooves and the auricles rather than posterior venous structures.

notes.A: The anterior interventricular groove separates the ventricular surfaces and contains the anterior interventricular vessels.
notes.B: The coronary sulcus separates atria from ventricles, with portions visible on the anterior surface.
notes.C: The right auricle projects anteriorly from the right atrium beside the ascending aorta.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below. Its opening is inside the atrium.
notes.E: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior coronary sulcus and drains into the right atrium.

ana-ms15-33.why: The right atrium receives systemic and coronary venous blood and contains the fossa ovalis with its raised limbus. Pulmonary venous openings belong to the left atrium, while chordae and infundibulum belong to ventricles.

notes.A: The pulmonary veins normally open into the left atrium and carry oxygenated blood from the lungs.
notes.B: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium near the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifice.
notes.C: The infundibulum is the smooth right ventricular outflow tract leading to the pulmonary valve.
notes.D: The limbus is the raised margin around the fossa ovalis on the right atrial side of the interatrial septum.
notes.E: Chordae tendineae connect atrioventricular valve cusps to papillary muscles within the ventricles.

ana-ms15-75.why: The epidermis consists of avascular stratified squamous epithelium. Its living cells obtain oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the underlying dermis rather than from vessels within the epidermis.

notes.A: The conjunctival connective tissue contains capillary networks that supply its overlying epithelium.
notes.B: The suprarenal gland has extensive capillary and sinusoidal networks that support hormone secretion into blood.
notes.D: Hepatic sinusoids are specialised discontinuous capillary channels that exchange substances with hepatocytes.
notes.E: Cortical bone contains blood vessels within central and perforating canals that nourish the mineralised tissue.

ana-ms15-76.why: Most central nervous system capillaries have continuous endothelium with tight junctions and restricted transcytosis. This specialised endothelial barrier helps maintain the stable extracellular environment required by neurones.

notes.A: Continuous capillaries lack endothelial fenestrations; fenestrated capillaries have pores that facilitate exchange.
notes.C: Pulmonary alveolar capillaries have continuous endothelium forming part of the thin air–blood barrier.
notes.D: Skin capillaries are predominantly continuous, whereas fenestrated capillaries are typical of endocrine and absorptive organs.
notes.E: Sinusoids have wider channels and discontinuous endothelial or basal lamina features, unlike ordinary fenestrated capillaries.

ana-ms15-77.why: The deep palmar arterial arch lies deep to the long flexor tendons near the metacarpal bases. Its depth and overlying tissues prevent routine clinical palpation as a superficial pulse.

notes.A: The radial artery is palpable at the anterior wrist just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.
notes.B: The superficial temporal artery is palpable where it crosses the zygomatic arch anterior to the ear.
notes.C: The facial artery is palpable where it winds around the mandible immediately anterior to masseter.
notes.E: Dorsalis pedis is palpable on the dorsum of the foot, usually lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

ana-ms15-t16.why: The first part of the subclavian artery lies medial to anterior scalene and normally gives the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk. The costocervical origin varies by side.

notes.A: The vertebral artery arises from the first part and ascends towards the cervical transverse foramina.
notes.B: The superior thoracic artery usually arises from the first part of the axillary artery, beyond the first rib.
notes.C: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part and descends along the internal anterior thoracic wall.
notes.D: The thyrocervical trunk originates from the first part and supplies cervical and scapular structures through its branches.
notes.E: The thoracodorsal artery usually branches from the subscapular artery, which arises from the axillary artery.

ana-ms15-t26.why: The electrocardiogram records electrical activity: the P wave reflects atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Intervals and segments help localise conduction abnormalities.

notes.A: A prolonged PR interval indicates delayed atrioventricular conduction, commonly at the atrioventricular node, rather than delayed sinoatrial firing.
notes.B: The T wave reflects the electrical recovery of the ventricular myocardium following depolarisation.
notes.C: The segment between the QRS complex and T wave represents the interval when most ventricular myocardium remains depolarised.
notes.D: QRS abnormalities generally reflect ventricular activation, conduction or myocardial changes rather than isolated left atrial disease.
notes.E: An absent or abnormal P wave usually reflects altered atrial activation or rhythm, not necessarily atrioventricular node dysfunction.

ana-ms15-t31.why: Valve sounds are heard best at characteristic chest-wall sites rather than directly over their anatomical positions. The aortic and pulmonary areas lie superiorly, while tricuspid and mitral areas lie more inferiorly.

notes.A: The aortic area is at the right second intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum.
notes.B: The pulmonary area is at the left second intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum.
notes.C: Tricuspid sounds are best heard near the lower left sternal border, typically the fourth or fifth intercostal space.
notes.D: Mitral sounds are best heard at the cardiac apex near the left fifth intercostal space and midclavicular line.
notes.E: The normal apex beat is usually felt in the left fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line.

ana-ms15-t36.why: An end artery supplies a territory without sufficient collateral arterial flow to sustain it after occlusion. Renal and splenic segmental arteries and the central retinal artery illustrate this vulnerability.

notes.A: Renal segmental arteries lack effective intersegmental arterial communications, so occlusion can cause a segmental infarct.
notes.B: Splenic segmental branches have limited effective collateral connections, making their territories susceptible to infarction.
notes.C: The penis receives communicating arterial branches, rather than being a classic example of end-arterial supply.
notes.D: The stomach has abundant arterial communications along both curvatures, providing collateral routes for blood flow.
notes.E: The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina with little effective collateral circulation.

ana-ms15-t91.why: Superficial veins and cutaneous arterial branches run within the thigh subcutaneous tissue. The saphenous opening, by contrast, is a defect in the underlying deep fascia lata.

notes.A: The great saphenous vein ascends superficially along the medial thigh before entering the femoral vein.
notes.B: The small saphenous vein usually ascends the posterior calf and terminates in the popliteal vein.
notes.C: The saphenous opening is a gap in fascia lata, which is deep to the subcutaneous tissue.
notes.D: The superficial epigastric artery ascends in superficial fascia towards the lower anterior abdominal wall.
notes.E: The superficial external pudendal artery crosses the superficial medial thigh towards the external genitalia.

ana-g16-a11.why: The deep palmar arch is formed predominantly by the radial artery and completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery. The superficial arch is predominantly ulnar.

notes.A: The ulnar artery chiefly forms the superficial palmar arch; its deep branch contributes to the deep arch.

ana-g16-a15.why: At the inferior border of teres major, the basilic vein continues as the axillary vein, receiving the brachial veins. The axillary vein becomes subclavian at the lateral border of the first rib.

notes.B: The lower border of teres major is the conventional landmark for the beginning of the axillary vein.

ana-g16-a19.why: The femoral sheath contains the artery laterally, the vein centrally and the femoral canal medially. The canal allows expansion of the adjacent femoral vein and contains loose tissue and lymphatics.

notes.A: The canal lies medial to both femoral vessels, rather than between the artery and vein.

ana-g16-a33.why: Paraumbilical veins accompany the ligamentum teres within the falciform ligament and communicate with the left portal vein. Their connections to superficial abdominal veins provide a portosystemic collateral pathway.

notes.B: Paraumbilical veins accompany the round ligament to the left portal system and can carry flow towards superficial abdominal veins in portal hypertension.

ana-g16-a42.why: Near the sixth intercostal space, the internal thoracic artery divides into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries. Anterior intercostal branches arise along the internal thoracic and musculophrenic routes.

notes.A: Anterior intercostal arteries are segmental branches. The internal thoracic artery ends by giving the superior epigastric and musculophrenic branches.

ana-g16-a45.why: The paired inferior phrenic arteries provide major arterial supply to the inferior surface of the diaphragm. Superior phrenic, intercostal and internal thoracic branches supplement the diaphragmatic circulation.

notes.A: Internal thoracic branches contribute through the musculophrenic and pericardiacophrenic arteries, but do not constitute the principal supply.

ana-g16-a52.why: The pulmonary valve projects behind the medial end of the left third costal cartilage near the sternum. Its sound is heard best in the left second intercostal space.

notes.A: The pulmonary valve has a left-sided surface projection, not one at the right third costal cartilage.

ana-g16-a53.why: During ventricular contraction, papillary muscles tense the chordae tendineae attached to atrioventricular valve cusps. This prevents the closed cusps from prolapsing into the atria under ventricular pressure.

notes.B: Papillary muscle contraction stabilises the valve cusps through the chordae tendineae rather than opening the valves.

ana-g16-a54.why: The atrioventricular bundle penetrates the fibrous cardiac skeleton and courses at the superior interventricular septum before dividing. The atrioventricular node, rather than the bundle, occupies the inferior atrial septal region.

notes.A: The bundle of His reaches the interventricular septum; the atrioventricular node is in the atrial septal region.

ana-g16-a56.why: The conus branch commonly arises early from the right coronary artery and supplies the right ventricular outflow tract. In some individuals it arises separately from the right aortic sinus.

notes.B: The conus artery typically branches near the origin of the right coronary artery to supply the infundibulum.

ana-g16-a72.why: The right ascending lumbar and right subcostal veins commonly unite to form the azygos vein. Their left-sided counterparts contribute to the hemiazygos vein, with variations in both origins.

notes.A: The right-sided union contributes to the azygos vein, whereas the hemiazygos vein originates on the left.

ana-g16-a79.why: In the usual arterial pattern, the basilar artery terminates by dividing into the posterior cerebral arteries. The internal carotid artery normally terminates as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

notes.A: The posterior cerebral artery normally arises from the basilar artery, although a fetal-type carotid supply is a recognised variant.

ana-g16-a91.why: Scrotal skin receives anterior scrotal branches from the external pudendal arteries and posterior scrotal branches from the internal pudendal artery. This differs from the arterial supply of the testes themselves.

notes.B: The femoral artery supplies anterior scrotal skin through external pudendal branches, and the internal pudendal supplies posterior skin.

ana-g16-a136.why: The aortic arch curves over the left lung root and pulmonary arterial bifurcation. The ligamentum arteriosum links the arch and pulmonary artery, while the phrenic and vagus nerves cross its lateral aspect.

notes.A: The pulmonary trunk divides beneath the aortic arch into right and left pulmonary arteries.
notes.B: The arch passes superior to the left lung root as it continues into the descending thoracic aorta.
notes.C: The ligamentum arteriosum joins the aortic isthmus to the left pulmonary artery immediately beneath the arch.
notes.D: The left vagus nerve crosses the lateral arch; its recurrent laryngeal branch loops beneath the arch.
notes.E: The left phrenic nerve crosses the lateral aspect of the arch anterior to the vagus nerve.

ana-g16-k86.why: Axillary nodes are organised into pectoral, subscapular, humeral, central and apical groups. Most lymph from the upper limb and breast passes through these groups before reaching the subclavian lymphatic trunk.

notes.A: Central nodes receive lymph from the pectoral, humeral and subscapular axillary groups.
notes.B: Humeral nodes lie near the axillary vein and drain most lymph from the upper limb.
notes.C: Supraclavicular nodes are located in the lower neck, beyond the axillary nodal groups.

ana-g16-t24.why: Superficial chest-wall lymph drains mainly to axillary nodes, while deeper intercostal tissues drain towards parasternal and intercostal nodes. Breast lymph may also reach supraclavicular nodes via higher nodal pathways.

notes.A: Most superficial thoracic lymph reaches axillary rather than parasternal nodes.
notes.B: Pectoral axillary nodes receive lymph from the superficial anterior thoracic wall and the supraumbilical region of the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.C: Deep intercostal tissues drain chiefly to intercostal and parasternal nodes rather than superficial axillary pathways.
notes.D: Breast lymph can reach supraclavicular nodes through apical axillary and other communicating lymphatic pathways.
notes.E: Superficial lymph from the upper back generally reaches subscapular axillary nodes rather than superficial inguinal nodes.

ana-ms15-98.why: Lymph converges through regional trunks into two principal collecting ducts, with considerable anatomical variation in their termination. Hundreds of lymph nodes filter lymph along these regional drainage pathways.

notes.A: The conventional named trunks include paired jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks, as well as the intestinal trunk.
notes.B: The thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct represent the two conventional main collecting pathways.
notes.C: The human body contains several hundred lymph nodes, commonly estimated at approximately six hundred.

ana-ms15-100.why: Primary lymphoid organs provide environments for lymphocyte development and antigen-independent maturation. B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow, while T-cell precursors migrate to the thymus for maturation and selection.

notes.A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes encounter antigens carried in lymph.
notes.B: Red bone marrow produces lymphocyte precursors and provides the site of B-cell development and maturation.
notes.C: The thymus provides the specialised environment for T-cell maturation and selection.

ana-ms15-t66.why: Regional lymphatic drainage follows characteristic nodal pathways before entering the major lymphatic trunks. Most breast lymph drains to pectoral axillary nodes, while head and neck lymph passes through cervical nodes.

notes.A: The right jugular trunk can join the right lymphatic duct or empty independently at the right venous angle.
notes.B: Humeral axillary nodes are deep within the axilla and receive lymph from superficial and deep upper-limb vessels.
notes.C: Subpyloric nodes drain towards hepatic and coeliac nodal pathways rather than directly to the lumbar nodes.
notes.D: The jugulodigastric node belongs to the upper deep cervical chain and receives lymph from pharyngeal structures.
notes.E: Most breast lymph reaches the pectoral axillary group, not the humeral group that principally drains the arm.

ana-gpq-26.why: Waldeyer’s ring is a collection of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts. It includes pharyngeal, tubal, palatine and lingual tonsillar tissue.

notes.A: The palatine tonsils lie in the lateral oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
notes.B: The lingual tonsil comprises lymphoid nodules at the posterior part of the tongue.
notes.C: The jugulodigastric node is a deep cervical lymph node that receives tonsillar drainage, not tonsillar tissue.
notes.D: Submental nodes drain structures such as the chin and lower lip rather than forming the pharyngeal lymphoid ring.
notes.E: Tubal tonsillar tissue surrounds the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube in the nasopharynx.

ana-gpq-76.why: Superficial inguinal nodes comprise a horizontal group below the inguinal ligament and a vertical group beside the great saphenous vein. They drain superficial lower-limb, lower abdominal and perineal territories.

notes.A: The horizontal group lies parallel to and just inferior to the inguinal ligament.
notes.B: The vertical group lies along the terminal great saphenous vein in the proximal thigh.
notes.C: External genital skin generally drains to medial horizontal nodes, while lateral nodes receive gluteal and lateral abdominal drainage.
notes.D: The medial horizontal group receives superficial lymph from the lower anterior abdomen. Lateral abdominal territories may drain to the lateral horizontal nodes.
notes.E: Most superficial lower-limb lymph reaches the vertical group, except some vessels accompanying the small saphenous vein.

ana-gpq-159.why: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium with its long axis approximately parallel to the tenth rib. Its visceral surface bears impressions from the stomach, left kidney and colonic flexure.

notes.A: The long splenic axis runs approximately along the tenth rib, between the ninth and eleventh ribs.
notes.B: The phrenicocolic ligament forms a supporting shelf beneath the inferior aspect of the spleen.
notes.C: The colic impression on the visceral surface is related to the left colic flexure.
notes.D: The gastric impression occupies the broad concavity between the hilum and superior border.
notes.E: The renal impression lies posterior to the hilum and contacts the upper left kidney.

ana-osa-51.why: Superficial lymph from the upper posterior trunk generally drains to the subscapular axillary nodes. These lie along the posterior axillary fold and pass lymph to central and apical nodes.

notes.A: Superficial inguinal nodes receive lymph chiefly from the lower trunk, perineum and superficial lower limb.
notes.B: Pectoral axillary nodes primarily receive lymph from the anterior thoracic wall and breast.
notes.C: External iliac nodes receive deep inguinal and pelvic drainage. Upper-back skin generally drains through the axilla.
notes.E: Deep cervical nodes principally drain head and neck structures rather than the upper posterior thoracic wall.

ana-g16-a34.why: Superficial lymphatic collectors generally accompany superficial veins in the subcutaneous tissues. Deep lymphatic vessels more often accompany major arteries and veins supplying or draining deeper structures.

notes.A: Superficial lymphatics are associated with superficial veins, while deep lymphatics accompany deeper neurovascular bundles.

ana-g16-a60.why: When a cisterna chyli is present, its upper end continues as the thoracic duct near the thoracolumbar junction. The duct enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus at approximately T12, while the reservoir's level varies.

notes.B: The cisterna chyli continues into the thoracic duct near the aortic hiatus when this lymphatic reservoir is present.

ana-ms15-55.why: The thyroid gland lies immediately anterior and lateral to the upper trachea. Enlargement, especially with retrosternal extension, can narrow or displace the tracheal lumen and compromise airflow.

notes.B: A thoracic aortic aneurysm can compress the intrathoracic trachea. Thyroid enlargement is a common cause of compression in the lower neck.
notes.C: Aortic coarctation is a narrowing of the aortic lumen rather than a typical compressive mass.
notes.D: A retropharyngeal abscess can obstruct the upper airway by bulging into the pharynx rather than primarily compressing the trachea.
notes.E: Horner syndrome reflects interrupted sympathetic innervation and is not itself a mass that compresses the airway.

ana-ms15-57.why: The inferior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by T12 and anteriorly by the xiphisternal region. Its posterior boundary lies lower than its anterior boundary, with the diaphragm closing the opening.

notes.A: The inferior aperture slopes downwards posteriorly because its vertebral boundary lies below the anterior boundary.
notes.C: The posterior boundary is formed by the twelfth thoracic vertebra rather than two vertebral bodies.
notes.D: The lateral boundaries are formed by the costal margins as well as the eleventh and twelfth ribs.
notes.E: The anterior boundary is the xiphisternal region, with the costal margins forming anterolateral boundaries.

ana-ms15-59.why: The anterior mediastinum is the narrow space between the sternum and fibrous pericardium. It contains connective tissue, lymph nodes, thymic tissue and small mediastinal vessels rather than vagal branches.

notes.A: Sternopericardial ligaments connect the fibrous pericardium to the sternum across the anterior mediastinum.
notes.B: Small mediastinal branches of the internal thoracic artery supply tissues within the anterior mediastinum.
notes.C: Thymic tissue or its fatty remnant is found in the anterior and superior mediastinum.
notes.E: Anterior mediastinal lymph nodes receive lymph from nearby mediastinal structures and connective tissues.

ana-ms15-60.why: The aortic arch lies above the transverse thoracic plane within the superior mediastinum. It connects the ascending and descending aorta and gives rise to the major arteries supplying the head and upper limbs.

notes.B: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve passes around the right subclavian artery near the root of the neck.
notes.C: The azygos arch lies in the superior mediastinum and enters the superior vena cava. The option names the inferior vena cava instead.
notes.D: The pulmonary trunk bifurcation lies near the transverse thoracic plane beneath the aortic arch in the middle mediastinal region.
notes.E: The right subclavian artery is a terminal branch of the brachiocephalic trunk near the right sternoclavicular joint.

ana-ms15-61.why: The right and left pleural cavities are separate potential spaces, each enclosed by its own continuous serous membrane. The mediastinum separates the two cavities rather than providing a normal communicating passage.

notes.A: Visceral or pulmonary pleura adheres closely to the lung surface and extends into its fissures.
notes.B: The visceral layer is continuous with parietal pleura at its reflection around the root of the lung.
notes.D: The endothoracic fascia lies between costal parietal pleura and the inner thoracic wall.
notes.E: Inflammation of pleural surfaces can produce fibrous adhesions joining the visceral and parietal layers.

ana-ms15-62.why: Pulmonary pleura is the visceral layer that covers the lung and follows its fissures. The parietal layer is named according to the thoracic region that it lines.

notes.A: The cupula is cervical parietal pleura extending above the first rib into the root of the neck.
notes.B: Mediastinal pleura forms the parietal covering of the lateral mediastinum and reflects at the lung root.
notes.C: Diaphragmatic pleura is the parietal layer over the diaphragm except where the mediastinum intervenes.
notes.D: Costal pleura forms the parietal lining of the internal rib surfaces and intercostal spaces.

ana-ms15-64.why: The main intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove of the rib above. Pleural aspiration uses the route above a rib to reduce injury to the main bundle, with ultrasound to identify a suitable site.

notes.B: The appropriate intercostal space depends on the indication, anatomy and imaging rather than a fixed seventh-space threshold.
notes.C: The access site is selected according to the intended pleural procedure and imaging, not simply because a midclavicular approach is convenient.
notes.D: A pleural drain connects to a closed drainage system to prevent unrestricted air entry into the pleural cavity.
notes.E: A sustained deep inspiration is not a routine requirement for pleural fluid aspiration or drainage.

ana-ms15-66.why: The vagus nerve descends posterior to the root of each lung, whereas the phrenic nerve descends anterior to it. This relationship is a useful landmark when studying the mediastinal surface.

notes.A: The hila and roots are situated approximately opposite the fifth to seventh thoracic vertebral levels.
notes.B: The phrenic nerve runs between mediastinal pleura and fibrous pericardium anterior to the lung root.
notes.D: The superior vena cava is a right-sided mediastinal structure related to the anterior aspect of the right lung root.
notes.E: The azygos arch curves above the right lung root before entering the superior vena cava.

ana-ms15-67.why: The lingula is a projection of the left superior lobe below the cardiac notch. It corresponds roughly to the right middle lobe and is absent from the right lung.

notes.B: The azygos vein arches over the right lung root and produces a groove on its mediastinal surface.
notes.C: The oesophagus is related to the posterior part of the right mediastinal lung surface and may leave an impression.
notes.D: The right superior lobar bronchus lies above the right pulmonary artery at the hilum and is termed eparterial.
notes.E: The superior vena cava is a right-sided mediastinal relation that produces an impression anterior to the hilum.

ana-ms15-68.why: The eparterial bronchus is the right superior lobar bronchus, which branches above the right pulmonary artery. On the left, the pulmonary artery arches superior to the bronchus at the hilum.

notes.A: The cardiac notch is an indentation of the anterior left lung border that accommodates the heart.
notes.B: The arch and descending thoracic aorta leave impressions on the mediastinal surface of the left lung.
notes.D: The lingula is a tongue-like part of the left superior lobe beneath the cardiac notch.
notes.E: The lower thoracic oesophagus can leave an impression near the inferior part of the left mediastinal lung surface.

ana-ms15-70.why: The right lung conventionally has ten bronchopulmonary segments, while the left often has eight or nine because some segments share bronchi. Each segment is supplied by a segmental bronchus and pulmonary arterial branch.

notes.A: The left main bronchus supplies two lobes through superior and inferior lobar bronchi.
notes.B: Lobar bronchi divide into segmental bronchi within the lung, supplying subdivisions of their respective lobes.
notes.C: A lobar bronchus supplies a lobe; a bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a segmental bronchus.
notes.E: A segmental pulmonary arterial branch normally accompanies each segmental bronchus, although arterial branching patterns vary.

ana-ms15-72.why: During forced expiration, abdominal wall muscles contract to raise intra-abdominal pressure and push the diaphragm upwards. This reduces thoracic volume, increasing alveolar pressure and driving air out.

notes.A: The scalene muscles elevate and stabilise the upper ribs during inspiration rather than forcing air out.
notes.B: External intercostals generally elevate the ribs during inspiration and help maintain thoracic wall stability.
notes.C: Diaphragmatic contraction increases vertical thoracic diameter during inspiration; relaxation permits the dome to rise during expiration.
notes.E: Sternocleidomastoid assists deep inspiration by elevating the sternum when the head and neck are stabilised.

ana-ms15-73.why: During pump-handle movement, the sternum and anterior ends of the ribs rise and move forwards, increasing the chest's anteroposterior diameter. Transverse expansion chiefly results from the bucket-handle movement of the ribs.

notes.A: Inspiration enlarges the thorax vertically, transversely and anteroposteriorly through coordinated diaphragmatic and rib movements.
notes.B: Bucket-handle elevation of the ribs moves their lateral portions outward, increasing the transverse diameter.
notes.C: As the diaphragm relaxes during expiration, its domes rise towards the thoracic cavity.
notes.D: Diaphragmatic descent increases the vertical diameter during inspiration, while ascent reduces it during expiration.

ana-ms15-74.why: Normal uncalcified costal cartilage is poorly distinguished on a plain chest radiograph because its attenuation resembles surrounding soft tissue. Calcification with age can make portions of the cartilage visible.

notes.A: The air-filled tracheal lumen produces a radiolucent central column against the mediastinal soft tissues.
notes.C: The diaphragmatic domes form visible curved interfaces between aerated lung and the abdominal soft tissues.
notes.D: The aortic arch creates the aortic knuckle, a visible contour of the left superior mediastinum.
notes.E: The main bronchi may be recognised as air-filled branching structures near the central pulmonary hila.

ana-osa-52.why: The target of thoracocentesis is the pleural space between the parietal and visceral layers. Entering visceral pleura would penetrate the lung surface rather than remaining within the intended space.

notes.A: Serratus anterior overlies the lateral thoracic wall and may be traversed in a midaxillary approach.
notes.B: The internal intercostal muscle forms an intermediate layer of the lateral intercostal wall.
notes.C: Parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall and must be crossed to enter the pleural cavity.
notes.E: Endothoracic fascia lies deep to the intercostal layers and superficial to the parietal pleura.

ana-g16-a61.why: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle occupies the costal groove along the lower edge of the upper rib. The route above the rib below reduces injury risk, while ultrasound identifies an appropriate site for pleural aspiration.

notes.B: The upper border of the lower rib is preferred over the lower border of the upper rib, where the main bundle runs.

ana-g16-p48.why: The rectum conventionally begins in front of the third sacral vertebra, where the sigmoid mesocolon ends and the three longitudinal muscle bands spread into a continuous outer layer.

notes.B: The prostate is related to the anterior wall of the lower male rectum, not its upper junction with the sigmoid colon.
notes.C: The obturator foramen lies in the anterolateral bony pelvis rather than at the posterior rectosigmoid junction.
notes.D: The urinary bladder lies anterior to the rectum and does not define its upper vertebral level.
notes.E: The pararectal fossae are peritoneal depressions beside the rectum, not the landmark defining its origin.

ana-g16-p61.why: The caudate lobe is on the visceral surface of the liver, posterior to the porta hepatis. It lies between the groove for the inferior vena cava and fissure for the ligamentum venosum.

notes.A: The quadrate lobe lies between the gallbladder fossa and the ligamentum teres fissure, anterior to the porta hepatis.
notes.C: The caudate lobe is a distinct posterior region rather than simply the back of the anatomical left lobe.
notes.D: The anterosuperior diaphragmatic surface is smooth and does not contain the principal landmarks of the caudate lobe.
notes.E: The porta hepatis separates the caudate lobe posteriorly from the quadrate lobe anteriorly.

ana-g16-k100.why: The pectinate line distinguishes the visceral sensory territory above from somatic sensory territory below. Internal haemorrhoids arise above this line and commonly bleed painlessly; thrombosed external haemorrhoids can be markedly painful.

notes.A: Visceral sensory innervation above the pectinate line contrasts with inferior rectal nerve supply below it.
notes.B: External haemorrhoids involve the external plexus draining through inferior rectal veins, not primarily the middle rectal veins.
notes.C: Internal haemorrhoids characteristically produce bright red rectal bleeding, whereas external haemorrhoids are especially associated with painful thrombosis.

ana-ms15-2.why: The lips consist of a muscular core of orbicularis oris covered by skin externally and mucosa internally. Their external landmarks include the philtrum and oral commissures, whose relationship to the teeth varies.

notes.A: The classical surface landmark for the oral fissure is the upper incisal edge, with variation according to posture and dentition.
notes.B: The philtrum is the vertical midline groove on the external surface of the upper lip.
notes.C: The oral commissure usually lies just anterior to the first premolar, although its level varies with facial and dental anatomy.
notes.D: Orbicularis oris surrounds the oral fissure and contributes to closing and protruding the lips.
notes.E: Labial mucosa contains minor salivary glands; ectopic sebaceous glands may occur but are not its principal glandular component.

ana-ms15-3.why: The cheek is the muscular lateral boundary of the vestibule, with buccinator supporting the mucosa and keeping food between the teeth. Like the lips, it has skin externally and oral mucosa internally.

notes.A: The cheeks bound the vestibule laterally and merge with the lips at the corners of the mouth.
notes.B: Buccinator takes origin partly from the pterygomandibular raphe, which also provides attachment for the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
notes.C: Facial nerve paralysis weakens buccinator, allowing food to collect between the cheek and teeth.
notes.D: Both cheek and lip have external skin, a muscular core and an internal mucosal lining.
notes.E: Masseter elevates the mandible outside the cheek wall; buccinator is the principal muscle of the cheek itself.

ana-ms15-4.why: Gingiva is masticatory mucosa surrounding the teeth. Attached gingiva is firmly bound to underlying tissue, and the junctional epithelium provides the epithelial attachment at the tooth surface.

notes.A: Attached gingiva lacks a distinct submucosa and is firmly connected to the underlying periosteum.
notes.B: The gingiva covers the alveolar process and surrounds the tooth neck, superficial to the coronal part of the periodontal attachment.
notes.C: The exposed gingival surface is commonly covered by keratinised or parakeratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
notes.D: At a healthy tooth with no attachment loss, junctional epithelium adheres to the enamel near the cemento-enamel junction.
notes.E: Cementoblasts deposit cementum on the tooth root, whereas gingiva develops as specialised oral mucosa.

ana-ms15-5.why: The oral cavity proper lies inside the dental arches and has a muscular floor formed principally by mylohyoid beneath the tongue. The hard and soft palate form its roof.

notes.A: The tongue occupies much of the cavity, while its underlying muscular floor is formed chiefly by mylohyoid.
notes.B: The oral fissure communicates with the vestibule, which in turn communicates with the oral cavity proper.
notes.C: The sublingual space lies immediately beneath the floor-of-mouth mucosa and contains the sublingual gland and related structures.
notes.D: The lingual frenulum marks the midline of the visible floor of the mouth, with a sublingual fold on each side.
notes.E: The soft palate forms the posterior portion of the roof and participates in separating the oral and nasal pharyngeal passages.

ana-ms15-8.why: The deciduous dentition contains twenty teeth, while the complete permanent dentition has thirty-two. The anatomical crown is enamel-covered; the clinical crown denotes the portion visible above the gingival margin.

notes.A: Each deciduous quadrant contains two incisors, one canine and two molars, totalling five teeth.
notes.B: Premolars occur in permanent dentition and replace deciduous molars during the transition to adult teeth.
notes.C: The clinical crown is the exposed part of the tooth, so its extent depends on gingival level.
notes.D: The cemento-enamel junction demarcates the anatomical neck between the enamel-covered crown and cementum-covered root.
notes.E: Enamel covers crown dentine; cementum instead covers the root dentine and provides periodontal ligament attachment.

ana-ms15-9.why: Extrinsic tongue muscles originate outside the tongue and move it as a whole. Genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus arise from bone, while palatoglossus arises from the palatine aponeurosis.

notes.A: Styloglossus arises from the styloid process and retracts and elevates the sides of the tongue.
notes.B: Genioglossus arises from the superior mental spine of the mandible and principally protrudes the tongue.
notes.C: Hyoglossus arises from the body and greater horn of the hyoid and depresses the tongue.
notes.D: The pterygoid process anchors muscles such as the pterygoids, not the standard extrinsic tongue muscles.
notes.E: Palatoglossus arises from the soft palate rather than directly from the bony hard palate.

ana-ms15-10.why: Human teeth are heterodont because they have distinct shapes adapted for different functions, and diphyodont because deciduous dentition is followed by permanent dentition. These terms describe separate aspects of dental organisation.

notes.A: Homodont dentition consists of broadly similar teeth, unlike the differentiated human incisors, canines and posterior teeth.
notes.B: Diphyodont dentition has two successive generations of teeth, represented by the deciduous and permanent sets.
notes.C: Haplodont teeth have a simple conical form, unlike the complex cusped posterior teeth of humans.
notes.D: Heterodont dentition contains different tooth classes adapted for cutting, tearing and grinding food.
notes.E: Polyphyodont dentition involves repeated generations of replacement teeth, rather than the two human sets.

ana-ms15-11.why: The stomach is divided into cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part, with the last subdivided into antrum and canal. Named notches and openings are landmarks rather than separate major regions.

notes.A: The cardia surrounds the gastro-oesophageal opening where food enters the stomach from the oesophagus.
notes.B: The incisura angularis is a notch on the lesser curvature that helps mark the boundary between the body and pyloric part.
notes.C: The body forms the large central region between the fundus and the pyloric part of the stomach.
notes.D: An isthmus is a narrow connecting region in other organs and is not a standard major gastric division.
notes.E: The term ampulla describes dilated regions such as the rectal ampulla, not a standard division of the stomach.

ana-ms15-12.why: Peritoneal folds suspend and connect abdominal viscera while providing pathways for vessels, lymphatics and nerves. The peritoneum itself is a serous membrane with a mesothelial lining and differing visceral and parietal sensory supply.

notes.A: Omenta extend from the stomach or proximal duodenum to other abdominal structures, as in the lesser and greater omenta.
notes.B: A mesentery is a double peritoneal fold suspending intestinal structures from the abdominal wall and transmitting their vessels.
notes.C: A peritoneal ligament is a fold joining an organ to another organ or to the abdominal wall.
notes.D: Parietal peritoneum has somatic innervation and is sensitive to local irritation, while visceral sensation chiefly responds to stretch and chemical stimuli.
notes.E: Peritoneal surfaces are lined by mesothelium, whereas endothelium lines blood and lymphatic vessels.

ana-ms15-13.why: The transverse mesocolon divides the greater sac into supracolic and infracolic regions. Peritoneal reflections partly restrict fluid movement, but communicating gutters allow fluid to spread between abdominal and pelvic spaces.

notes.A: The uterine tubes communicate with the peritoneal cavity, providing a potential route through the female reproductive tract.
notes.B: The subphrenic spaces lie between diaphragm and liver within the supracolic region of the greater sac.
notes.C: The falciform ligament limits direct subphrenic spread but does not prevent all communication between the two regions.
notes.D: The small-intestinal mesenteric root divides the infracolic spaces, while the left space opens inferiorly into the pelvis.
notes.E: The usual named right paracolic gutter is lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the pelvis inferiorly.

ana-ms15-14.why: The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Inferior extension into the greater omentum varies with fusion of its peritoneal layers.

notes.A: The traditional unfused inferior recess is more extensive; fusion of the omental layers can markedly reduce it in adults.
notes.B: The epiploic foramen provides the normal connection between the omental bursa and the greater sac.
notes.C: The caudate lobe is related to the superior part of the bursa, rather than the quadrate lobe.
notes.D: The inferior recess can extend between the layers of the greater omentum before their variable fusion.
notes.E: The left suprarenal gland is among the posterior relations of the bursa, separated by intervening peritoneum.

ana-ms15-15.why: The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach and lesser omentum and posteriorly by peritoneum covering retroperitoneal structures. It extends leftwards towards the spleen and communicates rightwards through the epiploic foramen.

notes.A: The splenic recess extends leftwards between peritoneal folds related to the spleen, including the splenorenal ligament.
notes.B: The right coronary ligament reflects around the bare area of the liver, rather than defining the right boundary of the lesser sac.
notes.C: The transverse mesocolon is related to the inferior boundary of the main lesser sac in the usual adult arrangement.
notes.D: The posterior wall includes peritoneum over the pancreas and diaphragm, separating these structures from the cavity.
notes.E: The posterior gastric surface and lesser omentum form much of the anterior boundary of the omental bursa.

ana-ms15-16.why: Intraperitoneal organs are invested by visceral peritoneum except at attachments such as a hilum or mesentery. The gallbladder and bladder have substantial uncovered surfaces, and most of the duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal.

notes.A: The spleen is invested by visceral peritoneum except at its hilum, where its vascular structures enter.
notes.B: The urinary bladder is predominantly subperitoneal, with its superior surface covered by reflected peritoneum.
notes.C: The vermiform appendix is intraperitoneal and is suspended by its vascular mesoappendix.
notes.D: Most of the duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal, with only its proximal portion freely mobile and peritoneally invested.
notes.E: The gallbladder surface attached to the liver lacks a complete serosal covering, unlike a freely invested intraperitoneal organ.

ana-ms15-17.why: Peritoneal investment varies according to an organ’s attachments and position. The liver has a bare area, most of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, and the uterus is only partly covered by reflected peritoneum.

notes.A: The sigmoid colon is conventionally intraperitoneal and suspended by its sigmoid mesocolon.
notes.B: The liver has uncovered regions including its bare area, porta hepatis and gallbladder attachment.
notes.C: The ovary projects into the peritoneal cavity. Specialised ovarian surface epithelium covers its free surface.
notes.D: Only the proximal duodenum is freely intraperitoneal; most of the remainder is fixed against the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.E: Peritoneum covers the uterine fundus and portions of the body but does not completely surround the cervix.

ana-ms15-18.why: The duodenum has four parts that curve around the pancreatic head. Its usual teaching length is approximately 25 cm, with the proximal bulb being mobile and most remaining segments fixed retroperitoneally.

notes.A: The combined four duodenal parts measure approximately 25 cm in the standard gross anatomy description.
notes.B: The proximal duodenal cap is mobile and differs from the predominantly retroperitoneal distal duodenum.
notes.C: The horizontal third part is conventionally about 10 cm long in the standard four-part description.
notes.D: The descending second part is commonly described as approximately 7.5 cm long in this teaching scheme.
notes.E: The ascending fourth part is conventionally about 2.5 cm long, although measured lengths vary between individuals.

ana-ms15-19.why: The jejunum occupies the proximal two-fifths of the mobile small intestine and generally has a thicker wall, longer vasa recta and less mesenteric fat than the ileum. Both regions are suspended by mesentery.

notes.A: The conventional length proportions are two-fifths jejunum and three-fifths ileum, excluding the duodenum.
notes.B: The jejunum has more prominent circular folds and a thicker wall than the distal ileum.
notes.C: Straight mesenteric vessels supply discrete territories in both regions. The greater number of ileal arcades does not guarantee collateral flow beyond a blocked straight vessel.
notes.D: Both jejunum and ileum are intraperitoneal and receive their vascular supply through the small-intestinal mesentery.
notes.E: Jejunal mesenteric fat typically stops short of the intestinal border, leaving translucent windows between vessels.

ana-ms15-20.why: The small-intestinal mesenteric root extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure towards the right iliac fossa. Its short attachment crosses major retroperitoneal structures while the free edge supports the mobile jejunum and ileum.

notes.A: The horizontal third duodenal part is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels and mesenteric root.
notes.B: The mesenteric root crosses the abdominal aorta as it descends obliquely to the right.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava lies behind the mesenteric attachment along its course across the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.D: The right ureter descends retroperitoneally behind the attachment of the small-intestinal mesentery.
notes.E: The right gonadal vessels descend along the posterior abdominal wall and are crossed by the mesenteric root.

ana-ms15-21.why: The colon is distinguished by three longitudinal muscle bands, haustra and fat-filled appendices epiploicae. Its luminal microbiota also participate in fermentation of material not digested by human enzymes.

notes.A: The colonic lumen contains an abundant microbial community that participates in fermentation and other metabolic processes.
notes.B: The outer longitudinal muscle of the colon is concentrated into three bands called the taeniae coli.
notes.C: Haustra are sacculations of the colonic wall associated with the arrangement and tone of its longitudinal muscle.
notes.D: Appendices epiploicae are small fat-containing peritoneal projections attached to the external surface of the colon.
notes.E: The taeniae converge at the appendiceal base and continue along the colon until they broaden at the rectosigmoid junction.

ana-ms15-22.why: The appendix is a blind-ended tube arising from the caecum below the ileocaecal opening. Its base is relatively constant, but the direction of its tip varies and is commonly retrocaecal.

notes.A: Appendiceal length varies considerably, with approximately 9 cm representing a traditional average in gross anatomy.
notes.B: The three caecal taeniae converge at the base of the appendix and provide a reliable anatomical landmark.
notes.C: The mesoappendix suspends the appendix and contains its principal arterial and venous supply.
notes.D: The appendiceal base opens into the caecum inferior to the ileocaecal orifice.
notes.E: The retrocaecal position places the appendiceal tip behind the caecum and is commonly described as the most frequent position.

ana-ms15-23.why: The rectum extends from approximately S3 to the anorectal junction at the pelvic floor. It is usually around 12–15 cm long, with its lower part dilated into the rectal ampulla.

notes.A: The rectosigmoid junction is conventionally located at the third sacral vertebra rather than the fourth.
notes.B: The anorectal junction lies near the tip of the coccyx, anterior to it where puborectalis encircles the bowel.
notes.C: The rectum is generally approximately 12–15 cm long, rather than a fixed length of 20 cm.
notes.D: The rectum lacks a free suspensory peritoneal mesentery, although its surrounding mesorectal connective tissue carries vessels and lymphatics.
notes.E: The ampulla is the dilated distal portion of the rectum, which accommodates faeces before defaecation.

ana-ms15-24.why: Peritoneum covers progressively less of the rectum as it descends. The conventional upper, middle and lower thirds have anterior and lateral, only anterior, and no peritoneal covering respectively.

notes.A: The posterior rectal surface and distal rectum are uncovered, so the entire organ is not intraperitoneal.
notes.B: The lateral surfaces of the upper rectum have peritoneum, and even the anterior covering ends at the lower rectum.
notes.C: The upper rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior and lateral surfaces but not posteriorly.
notes.D: The middle rectum retains an anterior peritoneal covering as the lateral reflection recedes.
notes.E: The lower rectum lies below the peritoneal reflection and is surrounded by pelvic connective tissue.

ana-ms15-36.why: Fungiform papillae are scattered among the much more numerous filiform papillae, particularly near the tip and margins of the tongue. They contain taste buds and have a rounded, mushroom-like profile.

notes.B: Filiform papillae cover much of the anterior dorsum and provide mechanical friction, rather than being confined mainly to the margins.
notes.C: Foliate papillae form folds on the posterolateral tongue rather than encircling the foramen caecum.
notes.D: Vallate papillae form a row immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis, not at the tip.
notes.E: Filiform papillae are mechanical papillae and lack taste buds; gustatory receptors occur in other papillae.

ana-ms15-38.why: The submandibular duct arises from the deep part of the gland and travels forwards in the floor of the mouth. It opens at the sublingual caruncle beside the lingual frenulum.

notes.A: The parotid duct emerges from the anterior border of the gland before crossing the lateral surface of masseter.
notes.B: The parotid duct crosses masseter superficially and turns medially to pierce buccinator before entering the oral vestibule.
notes.D: The sublingual gland drains mainly through multiple small ducts rather than having the largest major salivary duct.
notes.E: The sublingual gland commonly drains through multiple small ducts. Conventional sialography may miss these ducts, but their visibility depends on the imaging technique.

ana-ms15-41.why: The adult oesophagus is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the pharyngoesophageal junction at C6 to the gastric cardia near T11. Its length varies with body size.

notes.B: The oesophagus originates at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, approximately C6 rather than C4.
notes.C: The cervical oesophagus is usually directed slightly to the left of the midline as it descends.
notes.D: The oesophagus passes through the muscular oesophageal hiatus at T10, whereas the caval opening is at T8.
notes.E: The retropharyngeal and related retrovisceral spaces lie posterior to the pharynx and oesophagus rather than anteriorly.

ana-ms15-42.why: The thoracic oesophagus descends through the superior mediastinum before passing into the posterior mediastinum below the transverse thoracic plane. It enters the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus.

notes.B: The abdominal oesophagus is usually only about one to two centimetres long before joining the stomach.
notes.C: The right oesophageal border is continuous with the lesser curvature, while the left border meets the gastric fundus.
notes.D: The left vagus supplies most fibres of the anterior vagal trunk, while the right vagus contributes mainly to the posterior trunk.
notes.E: The left oesophageal border forms with the fundus an acute angle called the cardiac notch.

ana-ms15-43.why: The upper oesophageal constriction is at the pharyngoesophageal junction near C6, where the cricopharyngeus surrounds the passage at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

notes.B: The cricopharyngeal narrowing is encountered approximately 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth during endoscopy.
notes.C: The arch of the aorta crosses the oesophagus and produces one of its normal thoracic impressions.
notes.D: The aortic impression lies roughly 22–25 cm from the upper incisors, with variation between individuals.
notes.E: The diaphragmatic narrowing is encountered near 38–40 cm from the incisors, depending on body size.

ana-ms15-46.why: The round ligament of the liver occupies a fissure extending from the umbilical region to the visceral surface. Its course produces a notch in the sharp inferior border.

notes.A: The falciform ligament marks the lobar division on the diaphragmatic surface. The fissure for ligamentum venosum forms only part of the boundary on the visceral side.
notes.C: The bare area lies mainly on the posterosuperior aspect of the right lobe, where coronary reflections bound its direct contact with the diaphragm.
notes.D: The sharp inferior border separates the anterior diaphragmatic surface from the visceral surface rather than the posterior aspect.
notes.E: The gallbladder fundus commonly extends inferior to the liver margin near the right ninth costal cartilage.

ana-ms15-47.why: The falciform ligament is a double layer of peritoneum connecting the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. Its free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres.

notes.B: The triangular ligaments are lateral peritoneal reflections attaching the liver to the diaphragm on either side.
notes.C: The coronary ligament is reflected between the liver and diaphragm and defines margins of the bare area.
notes.D: The hepatogastric ligament forms part of the lesser omentum between the liver and lesser curvature of the stomach.
notes.E: The ligamentum teres is the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein within the falciform ligament.

ana-ms15-50.why: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum is a fibromuscular structure supporting the duodenojejunal flexure. Despite its common name, ligament of Treitz, it is not simply a double layer of peritoneum.

notes.B: The hepatogastric ligament is a double peritoneal layer connecting the liver with the lesser gastric curvature.
notes.C: The mesoappendix is a peritoneal mesentery carrying the appendicular vessels to the vermiform appendix.
notes.D: The gastrosplenic ligament is a peritoneal fold carrying short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels between stomach and spleen.
notes.E: The falciform ligament is a double peritoneal reflection connecting the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.

ana-ms15-52.why: The mesenteric root runs obliquely downwards and to the right from the duodenojejunal flexure to the right iliac region. Its direction is opposite to a course from right to left.

notes.A: The root separates the infracolic compartment into right and left spaces, with the right space on its right side.
notes.C: The horizontal third part of the duodenum lies posterior to the root of the small intestinal mesentery.
notes.D: The mesenteric root passes across the anterior surface of the right psoas major as it approaches the right iliac region.
notes.E: The inferior vena cava is among the retroperitoneal structures crossed by the small intestinal mesenteric root.

ana-ms15-53.why: The left lateral paracolic gutter extends down alongside the descending colon into the pelvic peritoneal cavity. Its superior communication is restricted by the phrenicocolic ligament, but it is not normally sealed inferiorly.

notes.A: The left paracolic gutter is the peritoneal channel lateral to the descending colon along the abdominal wall.
notes.B: The phrenicocolic ligament forms a barrier to upward spread of fluid from the left paracolic gutter into the left subphrenic region.
notes.C: The inferior opening of the left paracolic gutter permits peritoneal fluid to descend into the pelvic cavity.
notes.D: The gutter passes across the pelvic brim as it continues from the abdominal compartment towards the pelvis.

ana-ms15-54.why: The porta hepatis is the transverse fissure on the visceral surface through which hepatic ducts, vessels and nerves pass. It separates the caudate lobe posteriorly from the quadrate lobe anteriorly.

notes.B: The inferior vena cava groove lies on the right of the caudate lobe, while the ligamentum venosum fissure lies on its left.
notes.C: The colic impression lies on the visceral surface of the right lobe near the right colic flexure.
notes.D: The gastric impression is on the visceral surface of the left lobe where it relates to the stomach.
notes.E: The gallbladder fossa forms the right boundary of the quadrate lobe and the round ligament fissure forms the left boundary.

ana-ms15-78.why: Displacement of the stomach through diaphragmatic openings and reflux of its acidic contents are distinct anatomical and functional problems. Both can affect the upper gastrointestinal tract.

notes.A: A congenital diaphragmatic defect can permit abdominal viscera, including the stomach, to enter the thorax.
notes.B: A hiatus hernia involves migration of part of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.
notes.C: Pyrosis is the burning sensation commonly caused by reflux of acidic gastric contents into the oesophagus.

ana-ms15-79.why: The extrahepatic biliary system transports bile from the liver, stores and concentrates it in the gallbladder, and regulates delivery to the duodenum. Hepatocytes produce bile within the liver.

notes.A: The gallbladder stores bile and absorbs water and electrolytes to increase its concentration between meals.
notes.B: The sphincter of Oddi and gallbladder contraction regulate delivery of bile into the duodenal lumen.
notes.C: Hepatocytes and intrahepatic duct cells produce and modify bile. The extrahepatic biliary apparatus mainly stores, concentrates and conveys the fluid.

ana-ms15-80.why: Bile flows from intrahepatic canaliculi into progressively larger ducts, then through the hepatic ducts and extrahepatic biliary passages. The gallbladder communicates with this system via the cystic duct.

notes.A: The right and left hepatic ducts drain their respective hepatic territories and unite to form the common hepatic duct.
notes.B: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder neck to the common hepatic duct, allowing bile to enter or leave the gallbladder.
notes.C: Bile canaliculi are tiny intrahepatic channels formed between adjacent hepatocytes and are not extrahepatic ducts.

ana-ms15-81.why: The common hepatic duct forms from the right and left hepatic ducts, then joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct. The latter usually unites with the main pancreatic duct.

notes.A: The right and left hepatic ducts unite as the common hepatic duct before the cystic duct joins it.
notes.B: The junction of the cystic duct and common hepatic duct marks the beginning of the common bile duct.
notes.C: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct usually unite at the hepatopancreatic ampulla before opening into the duodenum.

ana-ms15-82.why: The gallbladder consists of a fundus, body and neck, which continues into the cystic duct. Hartmann’s pouch is a variable outpouching near the infundibulum or neck.

notes.A: Antrum is a standard subdivision of the pyloric stomach, not a conventional anatomical part of the gallbladder.
notes.B: The rounded fundus is the blind distal end of the gallbladder and may project below the liver margin.
notes.C: The gallbladder neck is a standard division. Hartmann's pouch refers to variable widening near the junction of the neck and body.

ana-ms15-83.why: The pancreas is divided into head, neck, body and tail, with the uncinate process projecting from the head. These anatomical terms describe its relationship to adjacent vessels and organs.

notes.A: The pancreatic head lies within the C-shaped curve of the duodenum on the right side of the abdomen.
notes.B: The elongated central portion of the pancreas is called the body, not the trunk in standard anatomical nomenclature.
notes.C: Rostrum is not a conventional subdivision of the pancreas; its left extremity is termed the tail.

ana-ms15-84.why: The main pancreatic duct drains the gland from tail towards head and usually joins the bile duct. The accessory duct, when patent, drains through the minor papilla above the major papilla.

notes.A: The accessory pancreatic duct generally courses superior to the terminal main duct and opens at the minor duodenal papilla.
notes.B: The main pancreatic duct begins in the tail and receives tributaries as it runs towards the pancreatic head.
notes.C: The ampulla is a ductal junction or dilation, whereas the major duodenal papilla is the mucosal elevation bearing its opening.

ana-ms15-85.why: The pancreatic body and tail receive branches of the splenic artery, while the head receives pancreaticoduodenal arcades connecting the coeliac and superior mesenteric territories. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.

notes.A: The splenic artery gives pancreatic branches along the superior border and supplies much of the pancreatic body and tail.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the head through the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery and its anastomoses.
notes.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies distal colonic and upper rectal territories rather than the pancreas.

ana-ms15-86.why: The pancreatic body lies retroperitoneally behind the lesser sac. Surgical exposure may be obtained through the gastrocolic ligament or transverse mesocolon, depending on the intended operation.

notes.A: The gastrocolic portion of the greater omentum can be opened to expose the lesser sac anterior to the pancreas.
notes.B: The transverse mesocolon provides an alternative anatomical approach to the region of the pancreatic body.
notes.C: The anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen contains the portal triad in the hepatoduodenal ligament and is not a standard access route.

ana-ms15-87.why: The elongated pancreas extends from the duodenal curve towards the splenic hilum. Its head, neck, body and tail are recognisable subdivisions, and its uncinate process projects from the inferior head.

notes.A: The pancreatic neck links the head and body and lies in front of the junction of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
notes.B: The pancreas is approximately 12–15 cm long in many adults, although its dimensions vary between individuals.
notes.C: The uncinate process projects medially from the inferior part of the pancreatic head, usually behind the superior mesenteric vessels.

ana-ms15-t76.why: Eruption usually begins with the lower central incisors and ends with the second primary molars before or around age three. The listed ages are teaching approximations, and upper and lower teeth have different reference ranges.

notes.A: The lower central incisors commonly erupt first at around six to ten months, with the upper pair following.
notes.B: Lateral incisors usually erupt after central incisors, and the lower lateral incisors may emerge several months into the second year.
notes.C: Primary canines commonly erupt during the second year of life after the first primary molars.
notes.D: The first primary molars typically emerge early in the second year, before the canines and second primary molars.
notes.E: Second primary molars complete the sequence, with reference charts giving ranges of about 23–31 months below and 25–33 months above.

ana-ms15-t141.why: Haematemesis is the passage of blood by vomiting, commonly from the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum. Coughing up blood is haemoptysis, so the route of expulsion distinguishes the two symptoms.

notes.A: Haemoptysis is expectoration of blood from the respiratory tract during coughing, rather than vomiting of blood.
notes.B: Haematemesis describes blood expelled by vomiting, commonly associated with an oesophageal, gastric or duodenal source.
notes.C: Haemothorax refers to accumulation of blood in the pleural cavity rather than bleeding through the mouth.
notes.D: A haematoma is a localised collection of blood within tissue or another confined anatomical space.
notes.E: Haemoperitoneum describes blood within the peritoneal cavity rather than the gastrointestinal lumen.

ana-gpq-114.why: The oral cavity is divided by the dental arches into vestibule and cavity proper. Its muscular floor supports the tongue, and its lining varies according to mechanical demands.

notes.A: The palatoglossal arches mark the lateral boundaries of the oropharyngeal isthmus at the posterior opening of the mouth.
notes.B: The oral vestibule lies external to the dental arches and internal to the lips and cheeks.
notes.C: Mylohyoid forms the principal muscular diaphragm of the mouth floor, whereas hyoglossus is an extrinsic tongue muscle.
notes.D: The vermilion zone of the lips lacks hair follicles and has superficial capillary loops contributing to its red colour.
notes.E: The hard palate and gingiva have masticatory stratified squamous epithelium, generally keratinised or parakeratinised for resistance to friction.

ana-gpq-116.why: A tooth has an anatomical crown and root, with dentine forming most of its structure. Enamel covers the crown, cementum covers the root, and vascular connective tissue occupies the pulp cavity.

notes.A: Dentine forms the bulk of the tooth and surrounds the pulp cavity beneath the enamel or cementum.
notes.B: The anatomical crown is the enamel-covered region, whereas the clinical crown is the part visible above the gingiva.
notes.C: Enamel is a highly mineralised tissue covering the anatomical crown and resisting the stresses of mastication.
notes.D: The dental pulp contains loose connective tissue, nerves and blood vessels within the central pulp chamber and root canals.
notes.E: Cementum covers the root dentine and provides attachment for periodontal ligament fibres anchoring the tooth in its socket.

ana-gpq-117.why: A complete permanent dentition has eight teeth per quadrant: two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. This gives a total of 32 teeth when third molars are present.

notes.A: The normal permanent quadrant contains two incisors and one canine, not three incisors and two canines.
notes.B: Two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars form the standard complete adult quadrant.
notes.C: A complete adult quadrant has three molars including the wisdom tooth, although third molars may be absent.
notes.D: The permanent quadrant has two incisors and two premolars rather than one incisor and three premolars.
notes.E: The permanent dentition contains two premolars per quadrant, so a formula with three premolars is incorrect.

ana-gpq-119.why: The primary dentition has 20 teeth that are normally shed as permanent successors erupt. Premolars succeed the primary molars, and permanent molars emerge behind them without primary predecessors.

notes.A: Primary tooth eruption usually starts near six months of age, most often with the lower central incisors.
notes.B: The second primary molars typically complete eruption by approximately two and a half to three years.
notes.C: The primary dentition has 20 teeth, compared with 32 in a complete permanent dentition.
notes.D: Normally, primary teeth exfoliate as their roots resorb and permanent successors erupt, although individual teeth may be retained.
notes.E: Permanent premolars replace the primary molars, while permanent molars erupt behind the primary dentition without predecessors.

ana-gpq-121.why: The oesophagus runs from the cricoid cartilage at C6 to the gastric cardia near T11, traversing the neck, thorax and a short abdominal segment. Its course shifts leftward towards the diaphragm.

notes.A: The oesophagus begins at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage around the sixth cervical vertebral level.
notes.B: The gastro-oesophageal junction is generally situated near T11, inferior to the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10.
notes.C: The adult oesophagus has an approximate length of 25 cm, with variation according to individual body dimensions.
notes.D: The portion between the oesophageal hiatus and gastric cardia is short, usually around one to two centimetres.
notes.E: In the lower thorax the oesophagus deviates leftwards and passes anterior to the descending thoracic aorta.

ana-gpq-123.why: Normal oesophageal impressions provide approximate endoscopic landmarks measured from the upper incisors. Their distances vary with body size, and the aortic and bronchial impressions may be described together.

notes.A: The cricopharyngeal narrowing at the upper oesophageal sphincter is approximately 15 cm from the upper incisors.
notes.B: The aortic arch produces an impression on the oesophagus around 22–25 cm from the upper incisors.
notes.C: The left main bronchus produces another thoracic impression approximately 25–28 cm from the incisors.
notes.D: The diaphragmatic impression is in the high thirties to about 40 centimetres from the incisors, depending on body size and landmark definition.
notes.E: The gastric cardia follows the short abdominal segment of the oesophagus, so it lies slightly distal to the diaphragmatic impression.

ana-gpq-124.why: The oesophagus has changing mediastinal relations as it descends. It initially lies behind the trachea, then passes behind the left main bronchus and anterior to several posterior mediastinal structures.

notes.A: The trachea lies anterior to the oesophagus throughout their shared course within the superior mediastinum.
notes.B: The left main bronchus, rather than the right, crosses anterior to the oesophagus and produces a normal impression.
notes.C: The thoracic duct ascends posterior to the oesophagus in the posterior mediastinum before crossing towards the left.
notes.D: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross towards the azygos vein posterior to the oesophagus.
notes.E: The cervical oesophagus lies anterior to the prevertebral fascia and associated retrovisceral connective tissue spaces.

ana-gpq-130.why: The root of the small intestinal mesentery extends from the duodenojejunal flexure to the right iliac region. Along this oblique course it crosses major retroperitoneal vessels and right-sided structures.

notes.A: The mesenteric attachment descends obliquely from the left side of L2 towards the right sacroiliac joint region.
notes.B: The root of the small intestinal mesentery crosses anterior to the horizontal third part of the duodenum.
