notes.C: The inferior vena cava lies behind the mesenteric root along its course towards the right iliac fossa.
notes.D: The mesenteric root crosses the right psoas major as it descends towards the right iliac region.
notes.E: The right ureter lies behind the mesenteric root along its course across the right posterior abdominal wall.

ana-gpq-131.why: The paracolic gutters are channels for peritoneal fluid between abdominal and pelvic spaces. The oblique root of the small intestinal mesentery restricts drainage from the right infracolic compartment more than from the left.

notes.A: The phrenicocolic ligament limits superior communication between the left paracolic gutter and the left subphrenic space.
notes.B: The right paracolic gutter communicates superiorly with the right subhepatic region, including the hepatorenal recess.
notes.C: The oblique mesenteric root restricts direct inferior drainage from the right infracolic space into the pelvis.
notes.D: The left infracolic space has inferior continuity with the pelvic peritoneal cavity, allowing fluid to track downwards.
notes.E: Fluid in the hepatorenal recess can descend along the right paracolic gutter towards the pelvis.

ana-gpq-132.why: The epiploic foramen provides the normal communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs. Its boundaries are important because the portal triad lies in the free anterior margin of the lesser omentum.

notes.A: The epiploic foramen opens at the right side of the lesser sac behind the hepatoduodenal ligament.
notes.B: The caudate process of the liver forms the superior boundary of the opening into the lesser sac.
notes.C: The superior first part of the duodenum forms the inferior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava covered by peritoneum forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
notes.E: The free right border of the lesser omentum contains the portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct.

ana-gpq-133.why: The four duodenal parts form a C-shaped loop around the pancreatic head. Conventional approximate lengths are 5, 7.5, 10 and 2.5 cm, with the proximal portion retaining mobility.

notes.A: The duodenum is conventionally about 25 cm long, although measured length differs among individuals.
notes.B: The superior first part of the duodenum is approximately 5 cm long from the pylorus to the superior flexure.
notes.C: The horizontal third part is conventionally around 10 cm long, approximately twice the length of the first part.
notes.D: The ascending fourth part is traditionally estimated at 2.5 cm, compared with about 7.5 cm for the descending part.
notes.E: Only the proximal two to two and a half centimetres of the first part retain the usual mobility and peritoneal investment.

ana-gpq-134.why: The duodenum begins near L1, descends on the right to approximately L3, crosses the midline and ascends to the duodenojejunal flexure on the left. Its horizontal third part is conventionally the longest.

notes.A: The superior duodenal part begins at the pylorus near the transpyloric plane at approximately L1.
notes.B: The descending second part passes along the right side of the upper lumbar vertebrae beside the pancreatic head.
notes.C: The horizontal third part crosses anterior to the aorta and inferior vena cava near the L3 vertebral level.
notes.D: The ascending fourth part passes to the left of the aorta towards the duodenojejunal flexure near L2.
notes.E: The third part is conventionally described as about 10 cm long, exceeding the usual 7.5 cm estimate for the second part.

ana-gpq-135.why: The horizontal duodenum crosses the posterior abdominal wall from right to left near L3. The superior mesenteric vessels cross anterior to it, explaining the possibility of compression between the artery and aorta.

notes.A: The right psoas major lies posterior to the right portion of the horizontal duodenum.
notes.B: The right ureter descends on psoas major behind the horizontal part of the duodenum.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava lies behind the horizontal duodenum on the right of the aorta.
notes.D: The right gonadal vessels descend on the posterior abdominal wall behind the horizontal duodenum.
notes.E: The abdominal aorta lies posterior to the horizontal duodenum, opposite the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly.

ana-gpq-136.why: The stomach normally lies mainly in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions, but its lower portion may extend into the umbilical region. Its position varies with posture, filling and body build.

notes.A: The distal gastric body and pyloric region commonly occupy part of the epigastrium.
notes.B: The liver and gallbladder occupy most of the right hypochondrium. The distal stomach is normally nearer the midline.
notes.C: The lower portion of the stomach may extend into the umbilical region, especially when distended.
notes.D: The stomach can descend below its upper abdominal position when full, but the central rather than the left lumbar region is its usual downward extension.
notes.E: The fundus and much of the gastric body occupy the left hypochondriac region.

ana-gpq-137.why: The gastric cardia is usually near T11, below the oesophageal hiatus at T10. The pylorus is commonly near L1 in the supine position, but gastric landmarks move with distension and posture.

notes.A: The gastro-oesophageal junction is typically near T11, while T10 corresponds to the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm.
notes.B: The pylorus commonly lies near the transpyloric plane at L1 when the stomach is relatively empty and the patient supine.
notes.C: The cardia lies to the left of the median plane where the oesophagus enters the stomach.
notes.D: The distance of approximately 40 cm from the incisors describes the cardia rather than the more distal pylorus.
notes.E: The greater curvature is usually above the umbilicus but may descend further when the stomach is distended.

ana-gpq-138.why: The stomach comprises the cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part. The angular notch on the lesser curvature helps distinguish the distal pyloric region from the body.

notes.A: The cardia is the small gastric region immediately surrounding the opening of the oesophagus.
notes.B: The fundus is the dome of the stomach projecting superior to the level of the cardiac opening.
notes.C: The body forms the largest gastric region between the fundus and the distal pyloric part.
notes.D: The angular notch occurs towards the distal lesser curvature at the transition from body to pyloric part.
notes.E: The pyloric antrum extends from the angular notch towards the narrower pyloric canal before the pylorus.

ana-gpq-142.why: The preceding case identifies an attached vermiform appendix, which arises from the posteromedial caecum below the ileocaecal junction. This attachment is much more specific than the mobility of an intestinal segment.

notes.A: The caecum receives the ileum and bears the vermiform appendix at the convergence of its taeniae coli.
notes.B: The ascending colon continues superiorly from the caecum but does not normally give origin to the appendix.
notes.C: The descending colon lies on the left posterior abdominal wall and does not bear the vermiform appendix.
notes.D: The transverse colon is mobile on its mesocolon but lacks a direct attachment to the appendix.
notes.E: The sigmoid colon is mobile in the lower abdomen and pelvis but does not carry the appendix.

ana-gpq-143.why: The appendix is identified by following the three caecal taeniae to their convergence at its base. Its narrow blind lumen and mesoappendix are useful additional features, while its tip position is variable.

notes.A: A blind ileal outpouching some distance from the ileocaecal valve suggests a Meckel diverticulum rather than the appendix.
notes.B: The appendix is a narrow blind-ended tube whose typical length is approximately five to ten centimetres.
notes.C: The three caecal taeniae converge at the appendiceal base, providing a reliable operative landmark.
notes.D: The retrocaecal position is common but not diagnostic because the appendiceal tip may occupy other positions.
notes.E: The mesoappendix is a triangular peritoneal fold that carries the appendicular artery and related vessels.

ana-gpq-146.why: Oncological colectomy removes the affected bowel and its draining mesocolon with the relevant vascular pedicles. The exact ligations depend on tumour location, anatomical variation and the extent of resection.

notes.A: A conventional right hemicolectomy removes terminal ileum, caecum, ascending colon and an adjacent portion of transverse colon.
notes.B: Transverse colectomy includes removal of the relevant transverse mesocolon and its regional lymphatic drainage.
notes.C: Right hemicolectomy involves the ileocolic pedicle and other appropriate colic vessels, not the right colic vessels alone.
notes.D: A standard segmental transverse colectomy follows the middle colic vascular pedicle. The vascular field differs if the resection extends to a flexure.
notes.E: Sigmoid colectomy includes ligation of the relevant sigmoid vessels arising from the inferior mesenteric vascular system.

ana-gpq-149.why: The classic hepatic lobule emphasises blood drainage towards a central vein, whereas the portal lobule emphasises bile drainage towards a bile duct. Blood and bile therefore travel in broadly opposite directions.

notes.A: The classic lobule is represented as a hexagon centred on a terminal hepatic venule, or central vein.
notes.B: Portal tracts at the lobular periphery contain branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
notes.C: The triangular portal lobule centres on a portal bile duct and incorporates portions of three neighbouring classic lobules.
notes.D: Hepatocyte plates extend radially between the central vein and the peripheral portal tracts, separated by sinusoids.
notes.E: Bile canaliculi are channels formed between adjacent hepatocyte membranes that carry bile towards peripheral ductules.

ana-gpq-151.why: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile beneath the liver. Its hepatic surface attaches to the liver, and its fundus projects towards the right costal margin.

notes.A: The gallbladder has a typical capacity of roughly 30–50 mL and concentrates stored hepatic bile.
notes.B: The fundus, body and neck are its usual gross divisions, with the neck continuing into the cystic duct.
notes.C: The hepatic surface attaches to the liver by connective tissue rather than having a complete free serosal covering.
notes.D: The fundus is classically projected near the right ninth costal cartilage at the transpyloric plane.
notes.E: Bile is produced by the liver, so after gallbladder removal it can still reach the duodenum through the bile duct.

ana-gpq-152.why: The gallbladder has absorptive simple columnar epithelium and an irregular smooth-muscle layer. Its mucosa concentrates bile and forms folds that become less prominent when the organ is distended.

notes.A: The muscular wall is relatively irregular, consisting of interlacing smooth-muscle bundles rather than a uniformly thick organised layer.
notes.B: The simple columnar lining has apical microvilli and absorbs water and electrolytes to concentrate bile.
notes.C: Mucosal folds vary with the region and degree of filling rather than maintaining a uniform appearance throughout.
notes.D: Typical gallbladder mucosa consists of absorptive columnar cells. Mucin-containing goblet cells can appear in intestinal metaplasia.
notes.E: Mucous glands are characteristically found in the neck rather than restricted to the fundus.

ana-gpq-154.why: Portosystemic anastomoses connect portal and systemic venous territories. In portal hypertension, these channels can enlarge and produce oesophageal varices, abdominal wall collaterals or other venous bypass pathways.

notes.A: At the lower oesophagus, left gastric tributaries communicate with oesophageal veins draining towards the azygos system.
notes.B: Veins near the bare area of the liver communicate with diaphragmatic systemic veins, allowing collateral drainage.
notes.C: The superior rectal venous territory communicates with middle and inferior rectal veins in the anal and rectal region.
notes.D: Paraumbilical portal tributaries communicate with superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall near the umbilicus.
notes.E: Veins of secondarily retroperitoneal bowel communicate with lumbar and other systemic veins along posterior abdominal wall attachments.

ana-gpq-155.why: The portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It ascends within the hepatoduodenal ligament posterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct.

notes.A: The main portal vein is commonly about eight centimetres long, although length varies between individuals.
notes.B: The portal vein lacks valves, allowing pressure changes to influence collateral venous flow in portal hypertension.
notes.C: The portal vein passes anterior to the inferior vena cava, with the epiploic foramen between them in the upper abdomen.
notes.D: The superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the main portal vein.
notes.E: In the free border of the lesser omentum, the portal vein lies behind both the bile duct and the proper hepatic artery.

ana-gpq-157.why: The pancreas is divided into head, neck, body and tail. Its neck overlies the formation of the portal vein, and its tail reaches the splenic hilum within the splenorenal ligament.

notes.A: The uncinate process projects medially from the inferior part of the pancreatic head behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
notes.B: The transverse mesocolon crosses the pancreatic head, so portions relate to both supracolic and infracolic compartments.
notes.C: The splenic and superior mesenteric veins unite behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
notes.D: The pancreatic body lies posterior to the peritoneal lining of the lesser sac, not freely inside that cavity.
notes.E: The pancreatic tail extends towards the splenic hilum between the layers of the splenorenal ligament.

ana-gpq-175.why: The rectum extends from approximately S3 to the anorectal junction. Unlike the colon, its longitudinal muscle forms a continuous layer, and its peritoneal covering becomes progressively more limited inferiorly.

notes.A: The rectal wall contains both inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle rather than circular muscle alone.
notes.B: The sigmoid colon becomes the rectum at approximately S3, below the level of the pelvic brim.
notes.C: Peritoneum covers the upper rectum anteriorly and laterally, the middle anteriorly, and leaves the lower rectum uncovered.
notes.D: The adult rectum measures roughly 12–15 cm from the rectosigmoid junction to the anorectal junction.
notes.E: The rectum lacks the characteristic haustra and appendices epiploicae of the colon and has a continuous longitudinal muscle layer.

ana-gpq-176.why: Digital rectal examination permits palpation of nearby pelvic structures through the rectal wall, including posterior bony landmarks and the anorectal ring. Structures higher in the pelvis are usually beyond reach.

notes.A: The coccyx is a posterior bony landmark that may be palpated through the lower rectal wall.
notes.B: In pelvic examination the ischial spines can be reached laterally through the rectal wall, depending on the anatomy and examination conditions.
notes.C: The anorectal ring corresponds largely to the puborectalis sling and sphincter complex at the anorectal junction.
notes.D: The rectosigmoid junction near S3 is generally too proximal for routine digital rectal examination.
notes.E: The sacral promontory lies near the pelvic inlet, usually beyond the reach of a finger inserted into the rectum.

ana-gpq-177.why: The upper anal canal has longitudinal columns linked inferiorly by valves that define the pectinate line. The epithelium and innervation change around this landmark, which also separates clinically important drainage territories.

notes.A: Anal columns are longitudinal mucosal folds in the proximal portion of the anal canal above the pectinate line.
notes.B: Anal valves are small folds connecting the inferior ends of adjacent anal columns.
notes.C: Anal glands drain into anal sinuses above the valves, and infection of these glands can cause abscesses.
notes.D: The pectinate line follows the lower margins of the anal columns and their connecting anal valves.
notes.E: The pecten below the pectinate line is covered by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium before the transition to skin.

ana-gpq-179.why: The ischioanal fossa is a fat-filled wedge beside the anal canal, allowing expansion during defaecation. Its lateral wall contains the pudendal canal, while its medial wall relates to the sphincter and pelvic diaphragm.

notes.A: Fat occupies most of the fossa, providing a deformable space that accommodates movement of the anal canal.
notes.B: The broad inferior base of the wedge-shaped ischioanal fossa is formed by the skin of the perineum.
notes.C: The medial wall is formed by the external anal sphincter inferiorly and levator ani superiorly.
notes.D: The ischial tuberosity and fascia covering obturator internus contribute to the lateral boundary of the fossa.
notes.E: The pudendal canal is a fascial tunnel on the lateral wall within obturator internus fascia, not in the skin-covered base.

ana-osa-99.why: The main pancreatic duct usually joins the common bile duct and drains through the major duodenal papilla. The papilla is on the medial wall of the descending second part of the duodenum.

notes.A: Pancreatic branches of the splenic artery supply much of the pancreatic body and tail.
notes.C: The superior mesenteric vessels lie between the pancreatic neck anteriorly and the uncinate process posteriorly.
notes.D: The common bile duct runs in a groove behind the pancreatic head or may be embedded in its substance.
notes.E: The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches along the anterior aspect of the pancreas near its anterior border.

ana-osa-100.why: Rectal portal-systemic collateral pathways connect the superior rectal vein with the middle and inferior rectal venous systems. These systemic veins eventually drain towards the inferior vena cava rather than joining it directly.

notes.A: Left gastric oesophageal branches form anastomoses with systemic oesophageal tributaries of the azygos venous system.
notes.C: Paraumbilical portal tributaries form anastomoses with superficial systemic veins of the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.D: Veins of the ascending and descending colon communicate with systemic lumbar veins along posterior abdominal wall attachments.
notes.E: Venous communications between the hepatic bare area and phrenic veins provide another potential route for portal-systemic collateral flow.

ana-osa-101.why: The right gastro-omental artery follows the greater curvature between layers of the greater omentum. The lesser omentum instead carries the gastric vessels along the lesser curvature and the portal triad in its free margin.

notes.A: The portal vein lies in the posterior part of the portal triad within the hepatoduodenal ligament.
notes.B: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature between the layers of the lesser omentum.
notes.C: The right gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature and anastomoses with the left gastric artery within the lesser omentum.
notes.E: The proper hepatic artery runs within the free right border of the lesser omentum alongside the bile duct and portal vein.

ana-osa-102.why: The epiploic foramen lies behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, the free right border of the lesser omentum. It connects the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs; the greater omentum does not form its anterior boundary.

notes.A: The opening occupies the right margin of the lesser sac and provides communication with the greater sac.
notes.B: The caudate process of the liver projects above the opening and contributes to its superior boundary.
notes.C: The superior first part of the duodenum lies below the foramen and forms its inferior boundary.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava, covered by peritoneum, forms the posterior boundary of the opening.

ana-osa-104.why: The lacunar ligament is a reflected triangular part of the inguinal ligament attached to the pecten pubis. It is aponeurotic tissue derived from external oblique, rather than a fold of peritoneum.

notes.A: The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the free right margin of the lesser omentum and connects the liver to the proximal duodenum.
notes.B: The coronary ligament is formed by peritoneal reflections between the liver and diaphragm bordering the hepatic bare area.
notes.C: The lienorenal ligament is a double layer of peritoneum connecting the splenic hilum to the posterior abdominal wall over the left kidney.
notes.D: The falciform ligament is a peritoneal fold attaching the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.

ana-g16-a57.why: Although the adult oesophagus is approximately 25 cm long, its upper end is at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage near C6, where the pharynx continues as the oesophagus.

notes.A: The quoted length is reasonable, but the oesophageal entrance is at C6 rather than C4.

ana-g16-a58.why: The abdominal oesophagus is a short segment between the diaphragmatic hiatus and the gastric cardia, commonly about 1–2 cm long. Its length varies with gastric distension and position.

notes.B: Only a short segment remains between the oesophageal hiatus and the gastric cardia, and their relative positions can change with filling.

ana-g16-a59.why: The aortic arch curves backwards and to the left of the trachea and oesophagus in the superior mediastinum. Its relationship to the oesophagus produces one of the normal oesophageal impressions.

notes.B: The aortic arch passes across the left side of the oesophagus, producing an impression distinct from the diaphragmatic constriction.

ana-g16-a62.why: The median umbilical fold overlies the urachus, now the median umbilical ligament. The paired medial umbilical folds instead cover the obliterated distal portions of the fetal umbilical arteries.

notes.A: The remnant of each umbilical artery lies in a medial fold, while the single median fold contains the urachal remnant.

ana-g16-a63.why: The epiploic foramen is the natural communication between the main peritoneal cavity and the omental bursa behind the stomach. It lies posterior to the free margin of the lesser omentum.

notes.B: The greater and lesser sacs are subdivisions of one peritoneal cavity, connected normally through this opening.

ana-g16-a64.why: The two layers of the left triangular ligament meet at the left end of the liver. Together they form a lateral peritoneal attachment to the diaphragm.

notes.A: The triangular ligament is at the lateral fusion of the peritoneal layers on the left, rather than the medial interval between anterior reflections.

ana-g16-a65.why: The greater omentum develops as a descending double peritoneal layer that folds back on itself, producing four layers that commonly fuse. The lesser omentum is formed from two layers.

notes.A: The reflected greater omentum has four developmental layers, whereas the lesser omentum is a two-layered fold.

ana-g16-a66.why: The right and left gastro-omental vessels run within the gastrocolic part of the greater omentum near the greater curvature. Their arterial branches anastomose and contribute to gastric blood supply.

notes.B: The two gastro-omental vessels follow the greater curvature in the gastrocolic part of the greater omentum, supplying the stomach and adjacent omentum.

ana-g16-a67.why: The aditus of the lesser sac is the epiploic foramen, also called the foramen of Winslow. This opening permits passage between the omental bursa and the greater peritoneal sac.

notes.B: The omental bursa communicates with the greater sac through the foramen behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, not through a gastric wall opening.

ana-g16-a68.why: The hepatorenal recess lies between the inferior surface of the right hepatic lobe and the upper right kidney. The inferior layer of the right coronary ligament limits its superior extent.

notes.A: The inferior coronary reflection separates the recess from the hepatic bare area, whereas the anterior reflection lies superior to that area.

ana-g16-a69.why: The right and left hepatic ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct. The cystic duct subsequently joins this duct to produce the common bile duct, which conveys bile towards the duodenum.

notes.A: The two hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct, and the common bile duct begins only after the cystic duct joins it.

ana-g16-a70.why: The main portal vein is commonly about 8 cm long, extending from the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins behind the pancreatic neck to its division near the porta hepatis.

notes.A: The usual textbook length of the main portal trunk is approximately 8 cm, although individual measurements vary.

ana-g16-a71.why: The uncinate process extends medially from the inferior pancreatic head and usually lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels. The pancreatic neck is anterior to these vessels near the portal venous confluence.

notes.A: The superior mesenteric artery runs in front of the uncinate process as it descends towards the root of the small-bowel mesentery.

ana-g16-a96.why: Peritoneal coverage of the rectum decreases inferiorly: the upper third is covered anteriorly and laterally, the middle third anteriorly only, and the lower third has no peritoneal covering.

notes.A: The middle third has anterior peritoneal coverage, unlike the entirely extraperitoneal lower third.

ana-g16-a99.why: The anorectal ring is a palpable muscular junction around the upper anal canal, with an important contribution from puborectalis. It is present in both sexes and helps maintain the anorectal angle.

notes.B: The ring can be assessed digitally through the anal canal in either sex because its principal muscular components are shared.

ana-g16-a106.why: The gastrosplenic ligament conveys vessels supplying the gastric fundus and upper greater curvature from the spleen. The splenorenal ligament, by contrast, conveys the main splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail towards the splenic hilum.

notes.A: The main splenic vessels approach the splenic hilum through the splenorenal ligament, rather than the gastrosplenic ligament.
notes.B: The pancreatic tail lies between the layers of the splenorenal ligament near the splenic hilum.
notes.C: The left gastro-omental vessels pass through the gastrosplenic ligament towards the greater curvature of the stomach.
notes.D: The short gastric vessels traverse the gastrosplenic ligament to supply and drain the gastric fundus.
notes.E: The left gastric vessels follow the lesser curvature within the lesser omentum rather than the gastrosplenic ligament.

ana-g16-a112.why: The lesser omentum connects the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum. Its hepatic attachment follows the porta hepatis and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum.

notes.A: The hepatogastric part attaches to the lesser curvature of the stomach along the gastric vascular arcade.
notes.B: The hepatic attachment extends upwards along the fissure containing the ligamentum venosum.
notes.C: The lesser omentum attaches around the porta hepatis, where the portal triad enters or leaves the liver.
notes.D: The hepatoduodenal part attaches to the proximal first part of the duodenum, approximately its first two centimetres.

ana-g16-a151.why: Several structures lie anterior to the abdominal aorta at different levels. In its upper part these include the posterior wall of the lesser sac and the pancreas. The left renal vein and horizontal duodenum cross further down.

notes.A: The lumbar arteries arise from the posterior aspect of the aorta and run laterally along the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.B: The right renal vein drains into the nearby inferior vena cava without crossing the aorta; the left renal vein crosses it.
notes.C: The upper abdominal aorta lies behind the posterior wall of the lesser sac near the origin of the coeliac trunk.
notes.D: The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna chyli through the aortic hiatus, posterior and usually to the right of the aorta.

ana-g16-p40.why: The ureters are muscular retroperitoneal conduits, not merely fibrous tubes. Their smooth muscle generates peristaltic waves that transport urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder independently of gravity.

notes.A: The ureters run outside the peritoneal cavity on the posterior abdominal wall and continue into the extraperitoneal pelvis.
notes.B: At the pelvic brim each ureter typically passes anterior to the common iliac bifurcation or an adjacent iliac artery.
notes.D: Each ureter has abdominal and pelvic portions of roughly comparable length, separated by the pelvic brim.
notes.E: The oblique intramural course allows rising bladder pressure to compress the ureter and limit retrograde urine flow.

ana-gpq-160.why: An adult kidney weighs roughly 150 g and measures about 10–12 cm in length. The liver displaces the right kidney inferiorly relative to the left, accounting for their slightly different surface landmarks.

notes.A: An adult kidney commonly weighs around 150 g, although weight depends on sex and body size.
notes.B: The right renal hilum usually lies slightly below the transpyloric plane, near the L1 level.
notes.C: The adult kidney is about 10–12 cm long; a length of 25 cm is much closer to that of the ureter.
notes.D: The left kidney is usually slightly longer, although individual renal measurements overlap and measurements in different axes can vary.
notes.E: The right upper pole lies near the lower thoracic vertebral levels, commonly around T12, rather than the upper border of T10.

ana-gpq-161.why: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, with similar muscular posterior relations but different anterior visceral relations. At the hilum the renal pelvis usually lies posterior to the main vessels, and perirenal fat surrounds the fibrous capsule.

notes.A: Both kidneys relate posteriorly to the diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis, with differences in rib relations.
notes.B: The typical anterior-to-posterior hilar arrangement is renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis.
notes.C: The second part of the duodenum and the right kidney are both retroperitoneal, with fascia rather than a peritoneal cavity between them.
notes.D: The hepatic impression on the right kidney normally relates to the liver across peritoneum in the hepatorenal region.
notes.E: Perirenal fat lies outside the fibrous renal capsule and inside the renal fascia, which encloses the fat.

ana-gpq-162.why: The subcostal neurovascular bundle and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross the posterior abdominal wall behind the kidneys. Other lumbar plexus branches take deeper or more inferior courses towards the lower limb.

notes.A: The subcostal vessels and nerve run below the twelfth rib and cross the posterior renal region.
notes.B: The iliohypogastric nerve crosses quadratus lumborum behind the kidney after emerging from the lateral border of psoas major.
notes.C: The ilioinguinal nerve follows a similar but more inferior route across quadratus lumborum behind the renal region.
notes.D: The femoral nerve descends between psoas major and iliacus towards the inguinal ligament rather than crossing the posterior renal surface.
notes.E: The obturator nerve descends medial to psoas major towards the pelvic wall and obturator canal.

ana-gpq-163.why: Renal cortex extends between the medullary pyramids as renal columns. Urine flows from collecting ducts at the papillae into minor calyces, then major calyces and finally the renal pelvis and ureter.

notes.A: The medullary pyramids appear striated because their tubules and collecting ducts run in approximately parallel bundles.
notes.B: The renal cortex lies immediately beneath the fibrous capsule and extends inward around the pyramids.
notes.C: Renal columns are cortical extensions between adjacent medullary pyramids and contain interlobar vessels.
notes.D: The renal papilla projects into a minor calyx, which collects urine discharged from papillary ducts.
notes.E: Minor calyces usually unite into major calyces before urine reaches the renal pelvis.

ana-gpq-166.why: Congenital renal variants include persistent lobulation, additional arteries, fusion anomalies and agenesis. Their reported frequencies depend on the population and diagnostic method, so approximate textbook figures should not be treated as exact prevalence estimates.

notes.A: Persistent fetal lobulation is usually a harmless contour variant. Recognising it on imaging helps distinguish it from scarring or a mass.
notes.B: Additional renal arteries are common anatomical variants, reported in roughly a quarter to a third of individuals.
notes.C: Horseshoe kidney is itself a relatively frequent fusion anomaly. Reported frequencies for polycystic kidney disease depend on subtype and how cases are found.
notes.D: Unilateral renal agenesis is congenital absence of one kidney and occurs in approximately one per thousand to two thousand births.
notes.E: Horseshoe kidney is a common renal fusion anomaly, reported in approximately one per five hundred to six hundred births.

ana-gpq-167.why: The urinary bladder has a superior surface and paired inferolateral surfaces when empty. Internally, its smooth trigone is defined by the two ureteric openings and internal urethral orifice.

notes.A: The interureteric ridge connects the ureteric openings and forms the upper boundary of the bladder trigone.
notes.B: The superior surface of the empty bladder faces upwards and is largely covered by peritoneum.
notes.C: The trigone is a smooth triangular mucosal area between the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening.
notes.D: The internal urethral orifice lies at the bladder neck and forms the inferior apex of the trigone.
notes.E: The paired inferolateral surfaces face the pelvic walls and are largely devoid of peritoneal covering.

ana-osa-56.why: Haematuria suggests injury to the urinary tract in this case. The inferior vena cava ascends to the right of the vertebral column, whereas the other structures are on the left near the kidney.

notes.A: Part of the stomach overlies the upper anterior surface of the left kidney, forming one of its left-sided visceral relations.
notes.B: The spleen occupies the left upper abdomen and lies against the upper lateral part of the left kidney.
notes.C: The left colic flexure lies near the anterior surface of the left kidney at the transition to the descending colon.
notes.E: The left suprarenal gland lies against the upper medial part of the left kidney within the renal fascial envelope.

ana-g16-a97.why: At the renal hilum the vein is usually most anterior. The renal artery lies behind the vein, and the renal pelvis lies behind the artery before narrowing into the ureter.

notes.B: The renal pelvis lies behind the main hilar vessels, with the renal artery behind the vein in the conventional arrangement.

ana-mic-smd-133-p5.why: The kidneys normally lie against the posterior abdominal wall, roughly between the twelfth thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae. A kidney in the pelvis represents an exception to normal ascent.

notes.A: Each kidney lies behind the parietal peritoneum, which makes it a retroperitoneal organ.
notes.B: A tough fibrous capsule lies directly on the renal surface, deep to the surrounding fat.
notes.D: The renal fascia encloses the perirenal fat and helps hold each kidney against the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.E: Peritoneum passes in front of parts of each kidney, although some adjacent organs contact the kidney without intervening peritoneum.

ana-mic-smd-134-p6.why: The hilum is the slit on the medial (concave) border through which the renal vessels, nerves and pelvis pass.

notes.A: A minor calyx receives urine from a renal papilla inside the kidney, well beyond the medial surface indentation.
notes.B: The renal pelvis collects urine from the major calyces and passes through the indentation on its way to the ureter.
notes.C: The ureter is the muscular continuation of the renal pelvis and carries urine towards the bladder.
notes.E: A renal pyramid is part of the medulla and ends at a papilla that projects into a minor calyx.

ana-mic-mic19-57-p15.why: The left kidney lies a little higher than the right, because the large right lobe of the liver pushes the right kidney down.

notes.A: The right kidney is usually lower because the large right lobe of the liver occupies space above it.
notes.C: Both kidneys occupy the posterior abdomen, but the more consistent difference is that the left upper pole lies higher.
notes.D: Both kidneys are retroperitoneal and lie on the posterior abdominal musculature, with the left usually positioned higher.
notes.E: The liver occupies more space on the right, so corresponding points on the kidneys usually lie at different heights.

ana-mic-mic19-58-p15.why: The kidney sits in a bed of fat enclosed by renal fascia. Pressure from surrounding abdominal contents and their peritoneal relationships also helps maintain its position during movement.

notes.A: The peritoneum overlies parts of the anterior renal surface, but this describes only one contribution to support.
notes.B: Neighbouring viscera help maintain renal position by contact and pressure, alongside the support provided by connective tissues.
notes.C: Renal fascia and surrounding fat provide structural support, while adjacent abdominal contents also help maintain position.
notes.D: Contact with viscera and the overlying peritoneum leaves out the renal fascia enclosing the fatty bed of the kidney.

ana-g16-p41.why: The urethra is widest and most dilatable while passing through the prostate. The membranous segment is relatively fixed where it traverses the external sphincter, and the external meatus has the smallest calibre.

notes.A: The preprostatic segment crosses the bladder neck, where smooth muscle forms the proximal sphincter around a short, relatively narrow passage.
notes.C: The membranous urethra traverses the external sphincter and has a relatively fixed calibre as it crosses the perineal membrane.
notes.D: The spongy urethra is the longest segment. Widening occurs locally at the bulb and within the glans.
notes.E: The external meatus is the opening at the tip of the glans and normally has the smallest calibre.

ana-g16-p42.why: Prostatic secretions reach the urethra through multiple small ductules. Their openings lie in the prostatic sinuses, the longitudinal grooves flanking the urethral crest.

notes.A: The prostatic utricle is a small blind pouch with a midline opening on the seminal colliculus.
notes.B: The paired ejaculatory ducts open on the seminal colliculus beside the utricle, distinct from the grooves receiving prostatic secretions.
notes.D: Each seminal vesicle drains through a duct that joins the ductus deferens before its secretion reaches the urethra.
notes.E: The bulbourethral glands release mucus through ducts that open further downstream in the proximal spongy urethra.

ana-g16-p44.why: Sperm enter the epididymal head from the testis and pass through the body to the tail. The epididymal duct continues from the tail as the ductus deferens.

notes.B: The ductus is a thick muscular component of the spermatic cord as it ascends from the scrotum.
notes.C: The spermatic cord carries the ductus through the inguinal canal towards the deep inguinal ring.
notes.D: Behind the bladder, the terminal ductus joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct.
notes.E: The ductus crosses above the ureter and its enlarged terminal part lies medial to the seminal vesicle.

ana-g16-p45.why: The bulbourethral glands drain independently into the proximal spongy urethra. Secretions from each seminal vesicle reach the prostatic urethra by a different route, through an ejaculatory duct.

notes.A: The rectovesical pouch extends between the rectum and the superior parts of the seminal vesicles.
notes.B: Seminal vesicles are secretory glands that add fructose-rich fluid to semen, whereas sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis.
notes.C: The paired glands lie behind the bladder base, with the anterior rectal wall immediately posterior to their fascial covering.
notes.D: Below the peritoneal reflection, a fascial partition separates the lower seminal vesicles and prostate from the rectum.

ana-g16-p51.why: The ischiocavernosus covers the crus of the penis, one of the erectile structures attached to the pubic arch. Both lie superficial to the perineal membrane.

notes.A: The prostate lies inside the pelvis beneath the bladder, surrounding the proximal course of the urethra.
notes.B: The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder and in front of the rectum, above the perineum.
notes.C: The membranous urethra traverses the external sphincter in the deep perineal region before reaching the bulb of the penis.
notes.D: The bladder neck is the pelvic outlet of the urinary bladder and is continuous inferiorly with the prostate.

ana-g16-p54.why: The obturator nerve primarily supplies the thigh adductors and a variable area of medial thigh skin. Scrotal skin receives anterior branches from the lumbar plexus and posterior branches from the sacral plexus.

notes.A: The ilioinguinal nerve emerges at the superficial inguinal ring and gives sensory branches to the anterior scrotum.
notes.B: The genital branch accompanies the spermatic cord and supplies the cremaster as well as part of the scrotal skin.
notes.C: The perineal branch of the pudendal nerve gives rise to posterior scrotal nerves supplying the back of the scrotum.
notes.D: The perineal branch of the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve supplies skin at the lateral and posterior scrotum.

ana-g16-p55.why: Each deep artery runs within a corpus cavernosum. Its helicine branches deliver blood into the erectile spaces when smooth muscle relaxes during erection.

notes.A: The tunica albuginea encloses the cavernous tissue, so the deep artery lies inside this fibrous covering.
notes.B: The deep fascia surrounds the erectile bodies and lies superficial to the deep arteries within them.
notes.C: The corpus spongiosum surrounds the urethra and receives arterial branches entering through the bulb of the penis.
notes.E: The prepuce is a fold of skin around the glans, anatomically separate from the paired cavernous bodies.

ana-g16-b6.why: The scrotum receives overlapping cutaneous branches. The ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves reach it from the inguinal region, while pudendal branches reach the posterior skin through the perineum.

notes.A: The ilioinguinal nerve gives anterior scrotal branches after emerging through the superficial inguinal ring.
notes.B: The genital branch travels with the spermatic cord and supplies part of the scrotal skin as well as the cremaster.
notes.C: Posterior scrotal nerves arise from the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve and carry sensation from posterior scrotal skin.

ana-gpq-168.why: The prostate surrounds the urethra just below the bladder and adds glandular secretions to semen. Its peripheral zone accounts for most of the glandular tissue and is a frequent site of carcinoma.

notes.A: The prostate lies superior to the perineal membrane, with its apex directed towards the external urethral sphincter.
notes.D: The peripheral zone accounts for the greatest volume of glandular tissue in the normal adult prostate.
notes.E: Most prostate carcinomas arise peripherally, but a tumour can also originate in another zone, including the transition zone.
notes.B: The broad superior surface is the base, where the bladder neck continues into the prostatic urethra.
notes.C: Prostatic secretions contribute roughly a quarter of ejaculate volume, with most of the remainder coming from the seminal vesicles.

ana-gpq-170.why: The ductus deferens leaves the inguinal canal at the deep ring and crosses the pelvic brim. It runs along the lateral pelvic wall before turning towards the bladder base and passing above the ureter.

notes.A: At the deep ring the duct curves around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric vessels before entering the pelvis.
notes.B: The duct passes across the external iliac vessels as it descends over the brim into the lesser pelvis.
notes.C: The duct runs medial to the obturator nerve and vessels as it traverses the lateral pelvic wall.
notes.D: The duct passes medial and posterior to the obliterated portion of the umbilical artery on its pelvic course.
notes.E: Near the bladder base the duct crosses the ureter from above before reaching the seminal vesicle.

ana-gpq-180.why: The male deep perineal pouch lies above the perineal membrane. It contains the urethral sphincter and bulbourethral glands, and neurovascular branches traverse this region on their way to the penis.

notes.A: The membranous urethra crosses the deep space and perineal membrane before entering the bulb of the penis.
notes.B: The distal internal pudendal vessels and their branches supply structures around and above the perineal membrane.

notes.A: The glans forms the distal expansion of the corpus spongiosum, while the bulb lies proximally at the root.

ana-g16-a95.why: The perineal membrane separates superficial from deeper structures. In the conventional description, the deep transverse perineal muscle lies on its superior side, while the superficial transverse muscle lies below it.

ana-g16-p46.why: The ovarian vessels approach the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall beneath a raised peritoneal fold. That lateral fold is the suspensory ligament of the ovary, also called the infundibulopelvic ligament.

notes.A: The mesovarium is the short posterior fold attached to the ovarian hilum, where a branch of the ovarian supply enters.
notes.B: The mesosalpinx supports the uterine tube along the upper part of the broad ligament and carries branches to the tube.
notes.C: The mesometrium is the broad lower part next to the uterine body, below the ovarian ligament and mesosalpinx.
notes.E: The transverse cervical ligament is a deep connective tissue support for the cervix and upper vagina near the uterine vessels.

ana-g16-p47.why: The suspensory ligament carries ovarian vessels from the lateral pelvic wall to the tubal pole. The opposite, uterine pole is tethered to the uterus by the ligament of the ovary.

notes.A: The round ligament connects the uterine cornu to the labium majus by passing through the inguinal canal.
notes.B: The ligament of the ovary joins its uterine end to the lateral angle of the uterus below the tubal opening.
notes.D: The transverse cervical ligament supports the cervix and upper vagina, anchoring them to connective tissue towards the pelvic wall.
notes.E: Lateral cervical ligament is another name for the transverse cervical support of the cervix and upper vagina.

ana-g16-p49.why: The perineal diamond runs from the pubic symphysis to the coccyx. Its posterior side boundaries follow the sacrotuberous ligaments, while the deeper sacrospinous ligaments run to the ischial spines.

notes.A: The inferior edge of the pubic symphysis is the anterior point where the two sides of the diamond meet.
notes.B: The inferior pubic rami form part of the ischiopubic arch along the anterior sides of the perineal diamond.
notes.D: The ischial tuberosities mark the lateral corners. A line joining them separates the urogenital and anal triangles.
notes.E: The ischial rami unite with the inferior pubic rami to form the anterolateral boundaries of the perineum.

ana-g16-p52.why: The female external urethral sphincter complex lies above the perineal membrane around the urethra. It includes striated muscle fibres that provide voluntary support for urethral closure.

notes.A: The crura of the clitoris lie below the perineal membrane and attach to the ischiopubic rami in the superficial compartment.
notes.B: The greater vestibular glands lie below the membrane near the posterior ends of the vestibular bulbs.
notes.C: Bulbourethral glands belong to male anatomy. Their female homologues are the greater vestibular glands in the superficial pouch.
notes.D: The vestibular bulbs are paired erectile tissues lying below the membrane on either side of the vaginal opening.

ana-g16-p53.why: The obturator fascia forms a channel along the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels travel within this channel to supply the perineum.

notes.A: The deep pouch lies above the perineal membrane and contains the urethral sphincter. The pudendal canal lies lateral to the ischioanal fossa.
notes.B: The superficial pouch lies beneath the perineal membrane and contains the roots of the external erectile structures.
notes.D: The broad ligament is a double layer of pelvic peritoneum extending from the uterus towards the lateral pelvic wall.
notes.E: The urogenital triangle is the anterior perineal region. The canal is a specific fascial tunnel along the lateral ischioanal wall.

ana-g16-p56.why: The uterine round ligament travels from the uterine cornu through the deep inguinal ring and inguinal canal. It passes out of the superficial ring and ends in the tissues of the labium majus.

notes.A: The suspensory ligament of the ovary carries the ovarian vessels between the tubal pole and the lateral pelvic wall.
notes.B: The ligament of the ovary attaches the medial ovarian pole to the uterus and remains within the pelvis.
notes.C: The female processus vaginalis is an embryonic peritoneal extension that usually closes. A persistent canal of Nuck is a variant.
notes.E: The suspensory ligament of the clitoris attaches its body to the pubic region close to the symphysis.

ana-g16-p59.why: A median episiotomy follows the midline between the posterior vaginal opening and the anus. The perineal body lies in this interval and receives fibres from several perineal muscles.

notes.B: The greater vestibular glands lie to either side of the posterior vestibule, lateral to the midline interval.
notes.C: The lesser vestibular glands are small mucous glands distributed around the vestibule, outside the central fibromuscular perineal body.
notes.D: The clitoris lies at the anterior end of the vestibule, well forward of the posterior vaginal opening.
notes.E: The urethral opening is anterior to the vaginal opening and lies away from the posterior perineal midline.

ana-g16-k87.why: Obstruction of superficial lymphatic drainage allows fluid to accumulate in the dermis. The skin swells while points tethered around hair follicles remain indented, producing the pitted appearance called peau d’orange.

notes.A: A blocked lactiferous duct obstructs secretion drainage from a lobule and can produce a local ductal swelling.
notes.B: Tumour involvement of dermal lymphatics impairs interstitial fluid clearance, leaving oedema around tethered skin structures.
notes.C: Glandular swelling can increase breast volume, while the pitted surface pattern arises from oedema within the skin.

ana-g16-k88.why: A tumour can infiltrate and contract the fibrous suspensory ligaments of the breast. Since these bands attach to the dermis, their shortening pulls a local area of skin inwards.

notes.A: Cooper’s ligaments link breast tissue to the dermis, so their contraction can retract the skin over a mass.
notes.B: Blocked dermal lymphatics produce diffuse oedema and the pitted appearance of peau d’orange.
notes.C: Swollen glandular tissue can contribute to a palpable mass, while a discrete overlying dimple reflects traction on the dermis.

ana-gpq-171.why: The tubal openings mark the upper lateral angles of the uterine cavity. The fundus arches above them, and the wider uterine body narrows inferiorly into the cervix and its canal.

notes.A: The fundus is the domed upper part of the uterus superior to the openings of the two tubes.
notes.B: Each uterine cornu is a lateral angle where the intramural part of the uterine tube opens into the cavity.
notes.C: The body forms the expanded upper part of the uterus and narrows towards the smaller cervix.
notes.D: The cervix forms the lower cylindrical part and projects into the upper part of the vagina.
notes.E: The internal os links the cervical canal to the cavity of the uterus, while the external os opens into the vagina.

ana-gpq-172.why: The cervix bridges the uterine cavity and vagina. The vaginal wall surrounds its lower part to form the fornices, and the pelvic ureter passes close to the supravaginal part.

notes.A: Peritoneum reflects over the posterior supravaginal cervix towards the rectum. The vaginal part projects below that peritoneal reflection.
notes.C: The ureter passes close to the lateral supravaginal cervix underneath the uterine artery, roughly one to two centimetres away.
notes.D: The external os is usually small and round in a nulliparous cervix and often becomes slit-like after vaginal birth.
notes.B: The vaginal wall attaches higher behind the cervix, making the posterior fornix deeper than the anterior fornix.
notes.E: The external os normally lies near the level of the ischial spines. Its position varies with uterine and pelvic support.

ana-gpq-173.why: The uterine tube extends from the uterine wall to a fimbrial opening near the ovary. Its medial segments are narrow, while the ampulla forms the broad, folded part where fertilisation usually occurs.

notes.E: The tubal mucosa contains ciliated and secretory simple columnar cells that support transport towards the uterus.
notes.A: The mature uterine tube measures approximately ten centimetres, although its length and course vary between individuals.
notes.B: The intramural portion passes through the uterine muscle and opens into the cavity at the cornu.
notes.C: The isthmus is the narrow segment immediately lateral to the intramural portion, nearest the uterus among the free segments.
notes.D: The ampulla is the longest and widest segment of the tube and has especially elaborate mucosal folds.

ana-gpq-174.why: The levator ani supports the pelvic organs from below. Connective tissue attached to the cervix and upper vagina provides additional support through the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments.

notes.D: The broad ligament is a mobile peritoneal fold and offers little resistance to downward displacement of the uterus.
notes.E: The round ligament helps maintain the forward position of the uterus and provides limited support against prolapse.
notes.A: The levator ani maintains pelvic floor tone and supports the vagina and uterus against downward displacement.
notes.B: The cardinal ligaments tether the cervix and upper vagina laterally and provide substantial connective tissue support.
notes.C: The uterosacral ligaments extend posteriorly from the cervix towards the sacrum, helping maintain apical support.

ana-g16-a100.why: Anteversion describes the inclination of the cervical axis relative to the vaginal axis. Flexion describes the angle at the junction of the uterine body and cervix, with forward bending termed anteflexion.

notes.A: The angle between the uterine body and cervix describes flexion, while version compares the cervix with the vagina.

ana-g16-a142.why: The uterine tube changes calibre along its course between the ovary and uterine cavity. The fimbrial infundibulum leads to the wider ampulla, followed medially by the isthmus and intramural portion.

notes.A: The short intramural segment traverses the uterine wall and opens into the cavity at the lateral uterine angle.
notes.B: The isthmus is a narrow, relatively thick-walled portion immediately lateral to the uterine wall.
notes.C: The infundibulum forms the lateral funnel, whose fimbriae project near the ovarian surface.
notes.D: The ampulla forms the wide, tortuous portion between infundibulum and isthmus and is the usual site of fertilisation.

ana-g16-a146.why: The broad ligament and its named subdivisions are reflections of peritoneum associated with the uterus, tube and ovary. The ovarian and round ligaments are fibromuscular remnants of the gubernaculum.

notes.E: The round ligament is a fibromuscular remnant that passes through the inguinal canal towards the labium majus.
