notes.B: The mesovarium is a short peritoneal fold extending backwards from the broad ligament to the ovarian hilum.
notes.D: The broad ligament consists of two layers of peritoneum reflected from the uterus towards the lateral pelvic wall.

ana-g16-a166.why: During labour the cervix shortens and thins as the opening widens. As the presenting part descends, it can press on the bladder and rectum and stretch the pelvic outlet.

notes.B: Effacement shortens the cervical canal as its tissue is taken up into the lower uterine segment.
notes.A: Cervical tissue thins with effacement while the external opening widens to permit passage of the presenting part.
notes.C: The descending presenting part can press the anterior bladder against the rigid pubic symphysis.
notes.D: The perineal body lies at the posterior vaginal opening and stretches as the presenting part reaches the outlet.
notes.E: The rectum lies behind the vagina and may be compressed by the presenting part during descent.

ana-g16-n62.why: The nucleus ambiguus supplies branchial motor fibres to the larynx and most muscles of the pharynx and palate through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Tensor veli palatini receives trigeminal motor fibres.

notes.A: Vagal fibres from the nucleus ambiguus supply the intrinsic laryngeal muscles through the superior and recurrent laryngeal branches.
notes.B: Stylopharyngeus receives branchial motor fibres carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve from the nucleus ambiguus.
notes.C: Vagal fibres to the pharyngeal plexus activate the constrictor muscles during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
notes.D: Palatoglossus receives vagal motor fibres through the pharyngeal plexus and helps narrow the opening to the oropharynx.

ana-g16-n63.why: The spinal part of the accessory nerve originates in the cervical spinal cord and supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The nucleus ambiguus in the medulla supplies branchial motor fibres carried chiefly by glossopharyngeal and vagal pathways.

notes.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries branchial motor fibres from the nucleus ambiguus to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
notes.B: The vagus carries fibres from the nucleus ambiguus to muscles of the palate, pharynx and larynx.
notes.D: The medullary fibres traditionally called the cranial accessory root join vagal pathways to the pharynx and larynx.
notes.E: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a vagal branch carrying branchial motor fibres to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

ana-g16-n67.why: An expanding pituitary adenoma can compress the optic chiasm above the sella. Nasal retinal fibres cross in its centre and carry information from the temporal visual fields, producing bitemporal loss.

notes.A: Complete loss of sight in one eye usually occurs with severe damage to its retina or optic nerve before the chiasm.
notes.B: Binasal loss would involve the uncrossed temporal retinal fibres at both lateral edges of the chiasm.
notes.D: A homonymous defect affects the same side of the visual field in both eyes and localises behind the chiasm.
notes.E: Macular sparing can accompany an occipital lesion in which the central visual representation remains intact.

ana-g16-n68.why: The nasal halves of both retinae receive light from the temporal visual fields. Their axons decussate in the centre of the optic chiasm, so a central lesion can remove both temporal hemifields.

notes.A: Each optic nerve carries input from one eye, so its injury causes monocular visual loss or a monocular field defect.
notes.C: The lateral chiasm carries uncrossed temporal retinal fibres, which represent the nasal field of the eye on that side.
notes.D: An optic tract carries the opposite visual hemifield from both eyes, making its loss homonymous.
notes.E: An optic radiation conveys one contralateral hemifield to the occipital cortex, so its lesions produce homonymous defects.

ana-g16-n75.why: The solitary nucleus receives taste and visceral afferents. Touch, pain and temperature from the anterior tongue instead enter trigeminal pathways via the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division.

notes.A: Chorda tympani fibres carry taste from most of the anterior tongue and project centrally to the rostral solitary nucleus.
notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior tongue and circumvallate papillae to the gustatory region of the nucleus.
notes.C: The internal laryngeal branch of the vagus carries epiglottic taste afferents towards the solitary nucleus.
notes.E: The caudal part of the solitary nucleus receives vagal afferents from thoracic and abdominal organs.

ana-g16-b7.why: Retinal signals travel in the optic nerve to pretectal nuclei, which project to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. Parasympathetic fibres travel with each oculomotor nerve, allowing one light stimulus to constrict both pupils.

notes.A: The optic nerve carries afferent input from the illuminated eye. Oculomotor parasympathetic fibres start the efferent limb.
notes.B: The pretectal area relays the reflex in the midbrain. The inferior colliculus chiefly relays auditory information.
notes.C: Bilateral pretectal output lets illumination of one eye produce direct constriction in that eye and consensual constriction in the other.

ana-g16-b9.why: At a chemical synapse, an electrical signal triggers transmitter release from one cell. The transmitter crosses a narrow extracellular gap and binds receptors that change the activity of the receiving cell.

notes.A: The presynaptic membrane has release sites where vesicles fuse and discharge neurotransmitter in response to calcium entry.
notes.B: The synaptic cleft is the extracellular gap through which transmitter diffuses before reaching the receiving cell.
notes.C: The postsynaptic membrane contains receptors that convert transmitter binding into an electrical or biochemical response.

ana-g16-b10.why: Free nerve endings lack a specialised capsule. A Merkel disc is an expanded sensory nerve ending associated with a Merkel cell in the basal epidermis, without the capsule typical of a corpuscle.

notes.A: Ruffini corpuscles have elongated connective tissue specialisations around endings that respond to sustained skin stretch.
notes.B: Free endings branch among tissue cells without a capsule and can signal pain, temperature or other stimuli.
notes.C: Merkel cell–neurite complexes lie near the basal epidermis and signal sustained indentation and fine spatial detail.

ana-g16-b11.why: Cutaneous receptors are tuned to different stimuli. Free endings include thermal and nociceptive sensors, while encapsulated mechanoreceptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles transduce distinct patterns of skin deformation.

notes.A: Pacinian corpuscles respond strongly to high-frequency vibration and rapidly changing pressure in deeper tissue.
notes.B: Different populations of free endings signal tissue injury, warming or cooling, and aspects of poorly localised touch.
notes.C: Meissner corpuscles respond to light moving touch in hairless skin and contribute to fine tactile discrimination.

ana-g16-b12.why: Muscle spindles encode muscle length and its rate of change. Primary and secondary spindle afferents carry that information to the spinal cord, while motor fibres adjust intrafusal tension or drive muscle contraction.

notes.A: Myelinated group Ia and II afferents carry signals from primary annulospiral and secondary flower-spray endings in the spindle.
notes.B: Gamma motor axons contract the ends of intrafusal fibres, adjusting spindle sensitivity during changes in muscle length.
notes.C: Alpha motor axons activate extrafusal fibres, which generate the main force of skeletal muscle contraction.

ana-g16-b13.why: The external capsule is a narrow sheet of white matter lateral to the putamen and medial to the claustrum. The extreme capsule is the separate white sheet between the claustrum and insula.

notes.C: The anterior limb of the internal capsule separates the caudate head from the lentiform nucleus.
notes.A: The putamen forms the lateral part of the lentiform nucleus and borders the external capsule medially.
notes.B: The claustrum is a thin grey sheet on the lateral side of the external capsule.

ana-g16-b18.why: The ventral medulla presents two corticospinal pyramids separated by the anterior median fissure. The roots of the spinal accessory nerve arise from the upper cervical cord.

notes.C: Spinal accessory rootlets arise along the lateral upper cervical cord and ascend into the skull through the foramen magnum.
notes.A: The anterior median fissure runs in the midline between the two ventral pyramids and is interrupted near their decussation.
notes.B: The pyramids contain descending corticospinal fibres and form paired elevations on the ventral surface of the medulla.

ana-g16-b19.why: The nucleus ambiguus is a medullary column of branchial motor neurons. Its fibres travel in glossopharyngeal and vagal pathways to muscles used in swallowing and phonation.

notes.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries motor fibres from the nucleus ambiguus to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
notes.A: Large motor neurons in the ventrolateral medulla form the longitudinal column called nucleus ambiguus.
notes.B: Damage weakens pharyngeal or laryngeal muscles, which can impair bolus propulsion and the protection of the airway during swallowing.

ana-g16-b20.why: The corpora quadrigemina are four elevations on the dorsal midbrain. The paired superior colliculi participate in visual orienting, while the paired inferior colliculi form part of the auditory pathway.

notes.B: The interpeduncular fossa lies on the ventral surface of the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.
notes.C: The longitudinal fissure divides the cerebral hemispheres and is separate from the dorsal surface of the midbrain.
notes.A: The quadrigeminal plate forms the tectum, which lies behind the cerebral aqueduct at the dorsal midbrain surface.

ana-osa-44.why: Axons of retinal ganglion cells collect at the optic disc and continue as the optic nerve. They are unmyelinated within the retina and acquire oligodendrocyte myelin behind the lamina cribrosa.

notes.B: Nasal retinal fibres decussate at the chiasm. The optic tract on the same side carries the temporal retinal fibres.
notes.C: The optic tract reaches the lateral geniculate body. Its relay neurons give rise to the optic radiation.
notes.D: The optic radiation passes through retrolenticular white matter to the visual cortex after synapsing in the lateral geniculate body.
notes.E: The medial geniculate body relays auditory signals. The optic radiation arises in the lateral geniculate body.

ana-osa-45.why: At the right lateral edge of the optic chiasm, uncrossed fibres carry signals from the temporal retina of the right eye. This retinal region receives images from the right eye's nasal field.

notes.A: Bitemporal hemianopia results from damage to crossing fibres from both nasal retinal halves at the centre of the chiasm.
notes.B: Binasal hemianopia requires disruption of uncrossed temporal retinal fibres on both sides, a rare pattern.
notes.D: Left nasal field loss involves temporal retinal fibres from the left eye, which remain on the left side of the chiasm.
notes.E: Complete right-eye blindness requires much more extensive loss of right-eye input, classically from a severe right optic nerve lesion.

ana-osa-106.why: Receptive aphasia typically follows damage to the dominant posterior temporal language network. Frontal lesions can instead disturb voluntary movement, gaze control, behaviour or speech production, depending on the site.

notes.A: Damage to the precentral motor cortex can produce contralateral weakness with upper motor neuron signs.
notes.B: Disruption of descending motor pathways in the frontal lobe can produce increased tone after the acute phase.
notes.D: A destructive frontal eye field lesion can impair voluntary conjugate gaze towards the opposite side.
notes.E: Prefrontal damage can alter judgement, initiative, inhibition and behaviour, producing a noticeable personality change.

ana-osa-107.why: Brodmann areas 44 and 45 occupy the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus. In the dominant hemisphere they form a core part of Broca’s language region.

notes.B: Areas one and two are parts of primary somatosensory cortex on the parietal postcentral gyrus.
notes.C: Areas 41 and 42 lie in the superior temporal auditory region, including cortex on the transverse temporal gyri.
notes.D: Areas 17 and 18 are primary and adjacent visual areas in the occipital lobe.
notes.E: Area five lies in the superior parietal lobule and contributes to somatosensory association.

ana-osa-108.why: Classic expressive aphasia localises to the dominant inferior frontal language region and adjacent pathways. Parietal lesions more typically affect cortical sensation, skilled movement or functions such as calculation and writing.

notes.A: Damage around the dominant angular gyrus can cause Gerstmann syndrome, including acalculia, agraphia and finger agnosia.
notes.B: The postcentral cortex processes fine spatial discrimination, which may be impaired on the opposite side after a parietal lesion.
notes.D: Parietal sensory damage can prevent identification of an object by touch despite enough primary sensation to feel it.
notes.E: Dominant parietal lesions can disrupt programming of learned movements, producing apraxia despite preserved basic strength.

ana-osa-109.why: Severe anterograde amnesia is associated with damage to hippocampal and related medial temporal circuits needed to establish new memories. Occipital lesions primarily disrupt visual fields or higher visual processing.

notes.A: A focal lesion in retinotopic occipital cortex can cause a local field defect, called a scotoma.
notes.B: Cerebral achromatopsia can follow damage to the ventral occipitotemporal network involved in colour perception.
notes.C: Prosopagnosia can follow damage to ventral occipitotemporal regions, particularly a right-sided network specialised for recognising faces.
notes.D: Injury to visual association cortex can prevent recognition of objects despite enough elementary vision to see them.

ana-osa-110.why: Astereognosis usually localises to the contralateral parietal somatosensory network. Temporal lesions can instead affect memory, understanding of language or auditory recognition, with the particular deficit depending on lesion location.

notes.A: Medial temporal structures, including the hippocampus, are needed to form new declarative memories.
notes.B: Damage around the dominant posterior superior temporal region can impair language comprehension and produce fluent, poorly meaningful speech.
notes.C: Temporal auditory association damage can prevent recognition of sounds even when basic hearing remains.
notes.E: Bilateral damage to primary auditory cortices in the superior temporal lobes can produce cortical deafness.

ana-osa-111.why: Clonus consists of rhythmic stretch-induced contractions due to exaggerated reflex activity after an upper motor neuron lesion. Lower motor neuron damage disrupts the motor limb of the reflex arc and reduces reflex activity.

notes.A: A damaged lower motor axon interrupts the reflex arc's efferent limb, so the corresponding tendon reflex decreases or disappears.
notes.B: Loss of motor input to the muscle reduces resting tone in the affected distribution.
notes.C: Denervated muscle fibres undergo pronounced wasting over time because they lose their normal neural input.
notes.D: Paralysis is flaccid when the final motor pathway to the muscle is interrupted.

ana-osa-112.why: Fibrillations and fasciculations suggest denervation of muscle fibres or motor units. An established upper motor neuron lesion more typically produces spasticity, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response.

notes.A: After the acute phase, loss of descending control can cause weakness with velocity-dependent resistance to passive movement.
notes.B: The muscle remains connected to lower motor neurons, so wasting is generally less marked than after denervation.
notes.C: Reduced descending inhibition can make tendon reflexes brisk and can allow repetitive stretch responses.
notes.E: In an adult, an extensor plantar response is a sign of dysfunction in the corticospinal pathway.

ana-osa-113.why: The Trendelenburg test assesses whether the hip abductors stabilise the pelvis during single-leg stance. Cerebellar assessment focuses on coordinated gait and limb movements, with sensory testing helping distinguish causes of ataxia.

notes.A: Tandem walking challenges balance and may reveal gait instability due to cerebellar dysfunction.
notes.B: The Romberg manoeuvre compares stance with eyes open and closed, helping distinguish sensory dependence from persistent cerebellar instability.
notes.D: Targeted finger-to-nose movement can reveal an intention tremor or difficulty judging distance in a cerebellar lesion.
notes.E: Moving the heel along the opposite shin tests coordination of the lower limb and may reveal cerebellar dysmetria.

ana-osa-114.why: Cerebellar disease impairs timing, calibration and coordination without usually causing primary paralysis. Limb findings from a cerebellar hemisphere lesion are generally ipsilateral, while midline disease more often affects stance and gait.

notes.B: Ataxia is impaired coordination that can make gait unsteady or limb movements irregular.
notes.C: Cerebellar involvement can disturb the timing and force of speech movements, producing dysarthria.
notes.D: Dysmetria is a failure to judge movement distance, so the limb overshoots or undershoots a target.
notes.E: Dysdiadochokinesia is difficulty performing rapid alternating movements smoothly and rhythmically.

ana-osa-116.why: The postcentral gyrus occupies the strip between the central and postcentral sulci. The supramarginal gyrus belongs to the inferior parietal lobule farther posteriorly, curving around the end of the lateral sulcus.

notes.A: The longitudinal fissure separates the cerebral hemispheres and borders the superior end of the postcentral gyrus.
notes.B: The central sulcus separates the postcentral sensory cortex from the precentral motor cortex in front of it.
notes.C: The postcentral sulcus marks the posterior limit of the postcentral strip and separates it from parietal association cortex.
notes.E: The inferior end of the postcentral region approaches the lateral sulcus, which separates it from the temporal lobe.

ana-osa-117.why: The dominant inferior frontal gyrus includes the opercular and triangular parts of Broca’s region. Damage here and in nearby networks can disrupt speech production, leading to effortful, nonfluent language.

notes.A: Anosmia is loss of smell and more commonly implicates the olfactory apparatus or its central projections.
notes.B: Contralateral lower facial weakness arises from damage to the face area of the precentral gyrus or its descending corticobulbar fibres.
notes.D: Apraxia is impaired performance of learned actions and can result from disruption of a wider parietofrontal network.
notes.E: Agnosia is failure to recognise a familiar stimulus despite adequate primary sensation, usually after association cortex damage.

ana-osa-118.why: Corpus callosotomy interrupts major connections between the cerebral hemispheres and can dissociate what each hemisphere can report. Phineas Gage’s reported behavioural change followed a frontal injury, a different anatomical mechanism.

notes.A: The corpus callosum carries interhemispheric fibres, so complete section reduces transfer of sensory and other information between hemispheres.
notes.B: In typical left language dominance, an object shown exclusively to the right hemisphere cannot be named through the usual left-sided language network.
notes.D: Without vision, an object felt in the left hand is represented initially on the right and may be inaccessible to left-sided language areas.
notes.E: When a laboratory task isolates information in one hemisphere, the patient's verbal report and actions may appear inconsistent.

ana-osa-119.why: An enlarging spinal cord syrinx can affect nearby anterior horn cells and descending motor pathways. These injuries can respectively reduce reflexes at the level of the cavity or increase them below it.

notes.A: A centrally placed cavity can interrupt the pain and temperature axons that cross in the anterior white commissure.
notes.B: Involvement of crossing fibres on both sides can cause bilateral loss of pain and temperature in affected segments.
notes.C: Dorsal column fibres can remain intact early, preserving vibration and joint position sense despite loss of pain and temperature.
notes.D: An extensive syrinx can injure descending motor tracts, leading to severe weakness of the lower limbs.

ana-osa-120.why: The internal capsule lies medial to the lentiform nucleus. Going laterally from the globus pallidus towards the insula, one passes through putamen, external capsule, claustrum and then extreme capsule.

notes.B: The external capsule is the thin sheet of white matter between the putamen and claustrum.
notes.C: The putamen is the lateral part of the lentiform nucleus, immediately lateral to the globus pallidus.
notes.D: The claustrum is a thin sheet of grey matter between the external and extreme capsules.
notes.E: The extreme capsule is the white matter layer between the claustrum and overlying insular cortex.

ana-g16-a75.why: Cranial dura has a periosteal layer and a meningeal layer, which separate to form dural venous sinuses. The spinal dural sac continues the meningeal layer and is separated from the vertebral canal by a true epidural space.

notes.B: A real epidural compartment containing fat and veins separates spinal dura from vertebral periosteum.

ana-g16-a76.why: The frontal, parietal and temporal opercula form lips around the lateral sulcus and overlie the insula. The gyrus rectus lies on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe medial to the olfactory sulcus.

notes.A: The gyrus rectus is on the underside of the frontal lobe rather than on a lip covering the insula.

ana-g16-a77.why: The superior surface of the thalamus contributes to the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle. It lies medial to the caudate nucleus, with the stria terminalis running along their interval.

notes.B: The superior thalamic surface forms part of the ventricular floor alongside the groove for the stria terminalis.

ana-g16-a78.why: The interventricular foramen links each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle. Its anterior margin is closely related to a column of the fornix, while the anterior thalamus lies posteriorly.

notes.A: The crura lie posteriorly near the hippocampi and converge into the body before the fornix divides into anterior columns.

ana-g16-a82.why: Subfalcine herniation moves the cingulate gyrus under the free edge of the falx cerebri. It can compress the anterior cerebral or pericallosal vessels near the displaced medial hemisphere.

notes.A: The superior petrosal sinus runs along the petrous ridge, away from the falcine edge beside the displaced cingulate gyrus.

ana-g16-a83.why: Transcalvarial herniation is displacement of swollen brain through a defect in the skull vault. At the foramen magnum, downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils is termed tonsillar herniation.

notes.A: The foramen magnum lies at the skull base. Downward movement of the cerebellar tonsils through it defines a different herniation pattern.

ana-g16-a84.why: The superior and inferior colliculi form the four elevations of the tectum on the posterior midbrain. The cerebral peduncles and intervening fossa are seen on the ventral surface.

notes.A: The cerebral peduncles form ventral prominences. The colliculi lie behind the cerebral aqueduct on the dorsal side.

ana-g16-a87.why: Brodmann area 4 in the precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. Area 6 includes premotor and supplementary motor areas, while area 8 includes the frontal eye field.

notes.A: Area 6 helps plan movement and area 8 includes gaze control. The chief primary cortical motor area is area 4.

ana-g16-a88.why: The pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus make up the classical Broca region. The posterior superior temporal cortex is traditionally associated with language comprehension.

notes.A: The superior temporal gyrus includes posterior auditory and language comprehension regions, while Broca’s region lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.

ana-g16-a89.why: Agraphaesthesia is failure to identify a figure traced on the skin despite sufficient primary sensory input. It usually points to impaired contralateral parietal processing of the spatial pattern.

notes.A: The parietal cortex combines tactile signals needed to recognise the traced figure, whereas frontal motor regions chiefly organise movement.

ana-g16-a90.why: Nasal retinal fibres from both eyes cross at the centre of the optic chiasm. They carry the temporal visual fields, so a central compressive lesion can produce bitemporal hemianopia.

notes.B: The crossing nasal fibres carry temporal field information from each eye, so central chiasmal compression can affect both temporal fields.

ana-g16-a121.why: Hippocampal fibres gather in the fimbria and continue into the paired crura. The crura join the body, which divides into columns projecting towards targets including the mammillary bodies.

notes.A: The body divides anteriorly into paired columns, with postcommissural fibres continuing towards the mammillary bodies.
notes.B: The crura converge beneath the corpus callosum to form the body of the fornix.
notes.C: The hippocampal commissure contains fibres passing between the two sides at the level of the crura.
notes.D: Each crus curves beneath the splenium as a continuation of the fimbria before joining the body.
notes.E: The fimbria forms where axons from the hippocampal surface collect along its medial edge.

ana-g16-c11.why: Oculomotor palsy weakens the muscle that elevates the upper eyelid and most extraocular muscles. A functioning lateral rectus and superior oblique then pull the eye outwards and usually downwards.

notes.A: Trochlear palsy weakens superior oblique and can cause vertical diplopia, while the upper lid elevator remains innervated.
notes.B: Abducent palsy weakens lateral rectus, so the affected eye has difficulty moving outwards and may rest medially.
notes.D: Loss of cervical sympathetic output causes mild ptosis and miosis, with the main extraocular motor nerves still working.
notes.E: The facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi. Its palsy impairs eyelid closure, with the upper lid elevator and extraocular muscles intact.

ana-g16-c12.why: The abducent nerve supplies the lateral rectus, which moves the eye laterally. The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique, and the oculomotor nerve supplies most of the other orbital muscles.

notes.A: The medial rectus adducts the eye and receives motor fibres from the oculomotor nerve.
notes.B: The superior rectus helps elevate the eye and is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes.C: The inferior rectus primarily depresses the eye and is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes.D: The levator raises the upper eyelid and receives motor fibres through the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.
